title: Overview
text: Overview Why simulation? It lets us try an action in a modeled world, calculate what happens, and repeat the experiment with different conditions. This free online book follows one familiar task: opening a drawer. We begin with how AI models understand instructions, then build the 3D object and describe how it moves. Simple explanations, illustrations, and moving examples connect these ideas. Language, vision, and robot actions — understanding a request, reading a picture, and choosing a movement. 3D representation, rendering, reconstruction, and generation — what is stored, how it becomes an image, and how methods create it. Articulated objects — parts, joints, and URDF files. Simulation — preparing a physical model, testing forces, and adding robot interaction.

title: 1. Language, vision, and robot actions
text: 1. Language, vision, and robot actions Explaining how to open a drawer, finding its handle in a picture, and commanding a robot to pull it require different abilities. This chapter uses the same cabinet to introduce three kinds of model: a large language model (LLM) , a vision-language model (VLM) , and a vision-language-action model (VLA) . We will compare what information each receives and what it produces. We will also distinguish understanding a picture from generating one, and see how an assistant can call another model to help with either task. One cabinet, three abilities Explain the task. Locate the handle. Choose an action. The inputs and outputs of the three cabinet examples Model Example input Example output LLM “How do I open a drawer?” Written instructions. VLM Cabinet image + “Where is the handle?” An answer based on the image. VLA Robot camera image + “Open the drawer.” Movement and gripper commands.

title: LLM: work with language
text: 1.1 LLM: work with language A large language model (LLM) learns patterns in language and can generate answers, explanations, or instructions. For the drawer task, we can describe the problem in words and ask it to suggest steps. Input: “How do you open a drawer?” Possible text output: “Hold the handle and pull outward.” This answer explains the task. With only that written request, the model has no picture showing where this cabinet’s handle is. Here, generating an answer means producing text . The term LLM describes language capability. Some models also accept images or other kinds of input; the next example uses that visual capability.

title: VLM: connect images and words
text: 1.2 VLM: connect images and words A vision-language model (VLM) combines visual information with language. Given the cabinet image and a question, it can connect the words “drawer handle” to a particular part of the picture. LLaVA [ 1 ] is one example: its image-processing component passes visual information to a language model. A chat example: add a cabinet picture A model that supports both text and images can handle either message below. The question stays the same; the information we provide changes. Words alone “Where is this cabinet’s drawer handle?” No picture or description identifies this cabinet. A possible reply: “Please send a picture or describe the cabinet.” Picture + words “Where is this cabinet’s drawer handle?” The image shows which part is the drawer. A possible reply: “On the blue drawer at the top.” These are illustrative replies. With the picture, the answer can refer to this cabinet , using visual information as well as words. One model can understand words and pictures LLM emphasizes language ability; VLM emphasizes combining vision and language. The labels can overlap. A model that handles more than one kind of information, such as text and images, is called multimodal . GPT-4o [ 2 ] , for example, was trained to process text and images within one model. When it receives the cabinet picture, it can use its own visual capability to answer. Uploading a picture therefore does not, by itself, mean that the application has switched models. Reading a picture and generating one Understand the cabinet picture Input: the existing picture + “Where is the drawer handle?” Output: “On the blue drawer at the top.” The task is to interpret what the supplied picture shows. Create a cabinet picture Input: “Draw a blue cabinet with a gold door.” Output: a new image of a cabinet. Editing is another image-generation task: supply a picture and ask to change the door’s color. Both tasks can appear in the same chat application. Their requested outputs are different: an answer about an image, or an image itself. OpenAI’s image guide [ 3 ] describes both uses. How can an assistant call another model? A chat application can connect its main model to other models through tools . The assistant requests a tool, and the application sends the required inputs to it and returns the result. This lets the assistant delegate a task. Call a VLM to read the picture Workflow Call a VLM to read the picture 01 Assistant requests help Ask a visual tool to locate the drawer handle. 02 VLM examines the image The application supplies the cabinet picture and question. The VLM returns a description of the handle’s location. 03 Assistant uses the result Answer: “On the blue drawer at the top.” This is an alternative to the main model reading the image itself. HuggingGPT [ 4 ] is a research example of an LLM selecting other models and using their results to compose a response. Call an image model to draw a picture Workflow Call an image model to draw a picture 01 Assistant requests an image Send “Draw a blue cabinet with a gold door” to an image-generation tool. 02 Image model creates it The model generates an image from the description. 03 Application displays it The new cabinet picture appears in the conversation. OpenAI’s image-generation tool [ 5 ] supports this arrangement: a main model can call a separate GPT Image model to generate or edit an image. Reading and drawing name the tasks. Calling a tool describes how the work is assigned. A model with its own vision capability can still call another model to create pictures.

title: VLA: produce robot actions
text: 1.3 VLA: produce robot actions A vision-language-action model (VLA) uses visual information and an instruction to produce robot actions. Depending on the model, it may also use information about the robot’s current position. For the cabinet task, the input is the robot’s camera image and “Open the drawer.” The output can be numbers telling its gripper —the robot’s grasping hand—where to move and whether to open or close. A robot controller turns those commands into signals for the robot’s motors. The next camera image shows what actually happened. Opening a drawer, step by step In this example, the gripper is already holding the handle. The diagram illustrates one possible action, not a recorded prediction from a trained model. 1 Camera image + instruction Drawer: 0 cm open Gripper: holding the handle Instruction “Open the drawer.” The image shows the current situation. The words give the task. 2 Process the image and instruction This example follows the broad structure of OpenVLA [ 6 ] . These components work together within the VLA. Inside a VLA Process an image and an instruction 01 Image encoder + adapter Turn the image into numerical features the main model can use. 02 Vision-language backbone Combine those features with the instruction “Open the drawer.” 03 Action output Produce action values. Here, a possible result is an outward movement with the gripper kept closed. 3 A possible command Move outward +0.10 m Gripper Keep closed In words: “Move the gripper 10 cm outward while holding the handle.” These are two readable fields for this one-direction example. A real robot’s command format can include more movement values. 4 Controller → movement → new image The controller tries to execute the command. If the drawer slides freely and the grip holds, the drawer can follow the gripper outward. Possible result: 10 cm open If the drawer is locked, it stays at 0 cm instead. The next camera image shows the actual result, so the next prediction can use that new information. ↺ The new camera image goes back to step 1. The model can then choose another action. What does “predict an action” mean? A VLA is trained using examples that pair observations and instructions with robot actions. It learns patterns in those examples. When given a new image and instruction, it uses what it learned to produce the next action values. For the same instruction, “Open the drawer,” different views can call for different commands: What the image shows Example next command The open gripper is positioned around the handle. Move 0 cm ; close the gripper to grasp it. The gripper is already holding the handle. Move 10 cm outward ; keep closed . These are illustrative commands. Here, “predict” means propose the next action . The structure is simplified from OpenVLA , whose predicted outputs are decoded into numerical robot commands. Other VLAs can organize their action outputs differently. What happens after the robot tries to pull? The VLA proposes a movement; the controller tries to carry it out. A freely sliding drawer may follow the gripper, while a locked drawer stays shut. The next observation helps the model choose what to do next. This interaction can happen with a real cabinet or in a simulation. In simulation, a physics engine calculates the movement, and a renderer produces the next camera image. Robot interaction in Chapter 4 explains how the model, controller, and simulator work together.

title: 2.1 Overview: 3D representations
text: 2.1 Overview: 3D representations A. Representation A photograph stores an image from one viewpoint. A 3D representation stores information about the cabinet in space, so software can inspect it or calculate views from other positions. This chapter separates three questions: what 3D data is stored , how that data becomes a picture , and how we obtain the data from photographs or a prompt . The same cabinet appears throughout. A. Representation 2.1–2.3 · What do we store? B. Rendering 2.4–2.6 · How do we make a view? C. Reconstruction and generation 2.7–2.10 · How do we create the 3D data?

title: What is stored?
text: 2.1.1 What is stored? A representation is a way of describing an object with data. For the same cabinet, we might save individual 3D points, connected surface patches, values in grid cells, soft colored blobs, or a function that answers questions about locations in space. The five examples below can describe the cabinet in 3D, but they store different information. Start with what each contains; the rendering group then explains how software uses it to draw a picture. The drawings below use one teaching cabinet: a teal body, a blue drawer, and a gold door. Both pull handles are fixed to their parts. The silver handle moves with the drawer; the gold handle moves with the door. We use these same parts in Chapter 3 . Point cloud Store: a list of 3D positions, sometimes with colors. Points can outline the drawer and handle. The list does not specify which points form a continuous surface. Mesh Store: 3D corner positions, called vertices, and surface patches, called faces, connecting them. The faces describe the cabinet’s surfaces. A face can have three sides (a triangle) or four (a quad). Voxel grid Store: values in small 3D cells, called voxels. Think of a pixel grid extended into depth. For this cabinet, each cell records whether its center lies in the cabinet material. We draw occupied cells as little boxes and leave empty cells clear. Smaller cells can capture thinner details, with more cells to store and process. 3D Gaussians Store: each blob’s position, size, orientation, opacity, and appearance. Each blob is a soft shape in 3D. Its opacity controls how strongly its color contributes and hides what is behind it. Many blue blobs can form the drawer’s image. Radiance field Describe: the color seen from a direction and the density at locations in 3D. Density controls how strongly a small region blocks the view. Near the drawer front, the answers may be blue and strongly blocking; in the air, almost no blocking. The dots mark example queries, not a stored point cloud. The voxel view uses the same cabinet geometry as the other examples. Its stepped outline comes from the size of the grid cells. These representations contain information in 3D. The image-making steps are grouped under Rendering, Sections 2.4–2.6 . Further reading: point clouds [ 1 ] , mesh structure [ 2 ] , 3D Gaussians [ 3 ] , voxel grids [ 1 ] , and NeRF’s radiance field [ 4 ] .

title: Representation, method, and renderer
text: 2.1.2 Representation, method, and renderer Making a 3D cabinet involves three different roles: a method creates the data, a representation specifies what is kept, and a renderer turns it into a picture. Representation What information do we keep? For example, the cabinet’s vertices and faces, or a set of 3D Gaussians. Reconstruction or generation method How do we obtain that information? Reconstruction tries to recover the cabinet seen in photographs. A generator can propose a cabinet using patterns learned from many examples, including guesses about unseen parts. Renderer How do we make a picture from it? Software uses the representation and a camera to calculate a 2D image. A method’s supported outputs depend on its design. Some methods produce surface geometry; some produce Gaussians; others support several representations. We first learn what those outputs contain, then follow how methods create them. For example: a method creates the cabinet as a mesh → we save its surface data → a mesh renderer draws a front view. The saved 3D data can also be used to draw a side view. A single method can support several output representations; TRELLIS in Section 2.10 is one example. The workflow map in Section 2.7 connects these roles and shows where rendering is reused during reconstruction.

title: Meshes: surfaces and useful detail
text: A mesh describes surface shape using connected patches . For a drawer, these can describe the outside, the inner walls, and the bottom. The empty space inside the drawer stays empty: a surface mesh does not mean the whole object is filled with material. A point cloud records sampled positions in 3D. A mesh also records how positions connect to form surfaces. The positions are called vertices, their connections are edges, and the surface patches are faces. Moving the positions changes the shape; changing their connections changes how the surface is assembled. Point cloud Useful for recording measurements. Gaps may mean an area was never observed, rather than a real hole. Triangle mesh Three-sided surface patches. Each triangle is flat, which makes its shape straightforward to calculate and draw. Quad mesh Four-sided surface patches. Regular rows can be convenient for editing. Software can divide them into triangles to draw the surface. Triangle and quad meshes on the same cabinet Both are surface meshes. In a quad mesh , each face has four sides. In a triangle mesh , each face has three. The cabinet below uses the same corner positions and camera in both views; only the face connections change. Quad faces Regular rows make it convenient to select and reshape a strip of the surface. Triangle faces Each four-sided patch here is divided into two triangles. The cabinet’s shape stays the same. Why use triangles or quads? Quads are useful for editing: rows of four-sided faces make it easier to select a strip of the cabinet surface and reshape it. Triangles are useful for rendering: three corners define a flat patch that software can project and draw. A common workflow is to edit with quads and let the software divide them into triangles for rendering. Blender’s triangulation tool. [ 1 ] Face type and amount of detail are two separate choices. A mesh can have a few large triangles or many small triangles; the same applies to quads. More, well-placed corners can follow a curved handle more closely, while more faces generally require more storage and processing. In the two cabinets above, splitting each flat quad into two triangles leaves the surface in exactly the same place. Measured points can be turned into a mesh by estimating a connected surface. Section 2.7.7 explains where this surface-reconstruction step fits. Why can a mesh look angular? A round bar has a curved surface. A mesh builds that surface from flat pieces . Imagine joining flat strips around the bar: a few wide strips make obvious corners; many narrow strips follow the curve more closely. 6 faces around the side Each face is wide. Look at the top edge: the bar has clear corners. 32 faces around the side Each face is narrower. The top edge comes much closer to a circle. Both models approximate the same round bar and use the same camera view. The lines show where the mesh faces meet. This is why the number of faces can matter: more, smaller faces can represent a curve more closely , when their corners are placed along that curve. A flat cabinet panel needs much less detail because its surface is already flat. More faces also mean more data to store and process. We choose enough to describe the shape we need; the highest face count is not automatically the best choice. The same idea on a cabinet These two cabinets have the same flat panels. Only the round handles change: each bar has 6 sides on the left and 32 sides on the right . The enlarged drawer handle makes the difference easier to see. 396 triangular faces 252 on the flat components + 144 on the handles. The round handles have visible corners. 1,020 triangular faces The same 252 flat-component faces + 768 handle faces. The handles follow the round shape more closely. The camera and colors are the same in both pictures. The lines mark the edges of the triangular faces. The extra faces improve the curved handles; the flat cabinet panels stay unchanged. For software used to inspect and edit these surfaces, see the 3D software guide .

title: 2.3 Gaussians and fields: representation
text: 2.3 Gaussians and fields: representation A. Representation A mesh records connected surfaces. Gaussians and fields describe the cabinet with other kinds of 3D data. First consider what they contain; the rendering group will show how that data produces a picture.

title: What a Gaussian representation stores
text: 2.3.1 Store soft 3D blobs 3D Gaussians: Representation · 2.3.1 · Rendering · 2.5 · Reconstruction with 3DGS · 2.8 A 3D Gaussian representation stores many soft 3D blobs. Each has a position, size, orientation, opacity, and appearance. The cabinet picture combines many blobs. One blue blob describes a small region near the drawer front. It can be wide along that panel but thin from front to back. Its contribution is strongest near its center and fades gradually toward the edges. One blob, enlarged. The curved lines help show its 3D shape. It covers only a small region of the drawer. 12 neighboring blobs. Each number marks one center. Gold center 1 identifies the same blob as on the left. 4,748 blobs in this example. Their colors blend into one cabinet image. The gold outline locates the small group shown in the middle. The first two views show shape guides so we can distinguish the blobs; their influence fades beyond those guides. The last view blends the blobs as a renderer does. This count belongs to our scripted teaching cabinet; different scenes use different numbers of Gaussians. 3D Gaussians names the stored elements. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) names the method studied later, which fits these elements to photographs and renders them by splatting. A generator can also produce Gaussian data. Original 3DGS project. [ 1 ] For now, keep the blobs fixed. Section 2.5 shows their projection and opacity with the two-blob and cabinet videos. A related method, 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) , uses flat Gaussian disks placed and oriented in 3D. The cabinet comparison in Section 2.8 shows how these surface elements differ from 3D Gaussian volumes.

title: Fields: ask about a location in space
text: 2.3.2 Ask a field about a location A field assigns information to locations in space. Imagine selecting a point inside a wooden cabinet panel, then another point in the empty drawer cavity. What the field answers depends on what it describes: Occupancy Is this point inside the solid shape? For a cabinet modeled with separate walls, a point inside the wood is occupied, while a point in the empty cavity is outside the solid material. A learned occupancy field can give a probability of being inside. Signed distance (SDF) How far is this point from the nearest surface, and on which side? With the convention used here, zero lies on the surface, negative is inside the solid, and positive is outside. A point in the cavity has a positive distance to the nearest wall. Radiance field What color and density are present here? In the cabinet example, the drawer front contributes blue and blocks the view; air contributes little. Color can also depend on viewing direction. These three fields answer different questions about the same cabinet. Occupancy and signed distance describe its shape; a radiance field supplies information for making pictures. Its density describes how a region affects visibility. Each kind of field can be implemented in different ways. Examples include Occupancy Networks [ 2 ] for occupancy, DeepSDF [ 3 ] for signed distance, and NeRF [ 4 ] for radiance fields. Radiance field: Representation · 2.3.2 · Rendering · 2.6 · Reconstruction with NeRF · 2.9 Example: NeRF represents a radiance field NeRF stands for Neural Radiance Field . It uses a neural network to supply the field’s answers: give it a 3D position and viewing direction, and it returns color and density. For our cabinet, samples near the drawer front can return blue with high density, while samples in the air return low density. This is one specific way to represent a radiance field. Section 2.6 follows how its answers become image pixels; Section 2.9 explains how photographs teach the network those answers.

title: Summary of A: a map of 3D representations
text: 2.3.3 Summary: a map of 3D representations We have described the same cabinet using points, connected faces, soft blobs, or answers at locations in space . This map brings those choices together. The voxel grid introduced in Section 2.1 stores values in small 3D cells. It also connects to fields: each cell can keep an occupancy or distance value. Representation map Ways to describe the same 3D cabinet Representation is the information kept about the object. Stored elements Point cloud 3D positions; optional colors. Mesh Vertices and connected triangle or quad faces. Voxel grid Values in small 3D cells, such as occupied or empty. 3D Gaussians Positions, sizes, orientations, opacities, and appearance. Fields: ask about a location Signed distance (SDF) How far from the surface, and on which side? Occupancy Is this location inside the solid, or how likely is it to be inside? Radiance field Density and view-dependent color. NeRF represents a field with a neural network. Storage and field meaning can be combined. A voxel grid can store sampled distance or occupancy values. A field describes what we can ask; its storage describes how the answers are kept. For example, a voxel grid can store an occupancy value in every cell. Representation tells us what 3D information is available. In Part B: Rendering , we use that information and a virtual camera to make a picture.

title: 2.4 Meshes: rendering with a camera
text: 2.4 Meshes: rendering with a camera B. Rendering Rendering goes from 3D to 2D. Start with a stored 3D cabinet, choose a virtual camera, and use a renderer to calculate the picture from that viewpoint. Workflow From a 3D scene to a 2D image 01 3D scene The cabinet and its appearance 02 Camera + renderer Choose a view and calculate its pixels 03 2D image A picture of the cabinet Mesh: Representation · 2.2 · Rendering · 2.4 · Reconstruction · 2.7.7

title: Render mesh surfaces
text: 2.4.1 Render mesh surfaces Sections 2.1 and 2.2 described the stored data. Rendering starts with that data already available and asks what a camera would see. A mesh supplies the surfaces of objects in a scene . A scene also specifies where those objects are placed, where the camera looks, and how surfaces are colored and lit. The renderer uses that information to calculate an image. A texture is often an image placed on a surface, like a printed pattern. A material controls how the surface responds to light—for example, whether a handle looks like dull plastic or shiny metal. Which tool makes these pictures? A renderer is the software that calculates the picture. We give it a 3D scene and a virtual camera: where the camera is, which way it looks, and how wide its view is. The software calculates the pixels and saves the result as an image. Think of photographing a cabinet from the left, front, and right. In rendering, we place a virtual camera at those three positions. We keep the same 3D cabinet and calculate a new picture from each position. For an example in a 3D application, see the Blender modeling and rendering example , which shows a mesh, camera viewpoints, and the rendered picture. What we have Example tool What we do A mesh Blender , using a renderer such as Eevee or Cycles. Load the model, set its appearance, place lights and a camera, then render and save an image. 3D Gaussians A Gaussian renderer, such as gsplat [ 1 ] . Load the blobs and choose a camera. The renderer projects the blobs and blends their colors into the image. A trained NeRF A NeRF volume renderer, such as the one in the original NeRF implementation [ 2 ] . Load the trained network and choose a camera. Query color and density along camera rays, then combine the answers into pixels. For this book’s Gaussian cabinet videos, we wrote a small renderer in Python. It calculates the projected marks and their color mixtures. The left, front, and right pictures all come from the same cabinet data. Rendering many frames while moving the camera, then joining those frames into a video, gives the moving-camera example . A screenshot can record a picture already displayed by a viewer. Here, the renderer saves its calculated images directly. Stored surfaces The mesh gives the cabinet its shape and depth. One camera view The surfaces become colored areas in an image. The construction edges need not be visible. One common mesh-rendering process is rasterization : Project the triangles. Use the camera’s position, viewing direction, and lens to map their 3D corners to 2D image positions. With a perspective camera, a farther object generally appears smaller. Find what each pixel sees. Work out which projected triangles cover it. For opaque surfaces, keep the nearest visible surface; a closed door hides what is behind it. Calculate the color. Use the visible surface’s material, texture, direction, and lighting. Repeat across the image. Imagine walking around a real cabinet: the cabinet stays still, but you see a different side. A virtual camera works similarly. Keep the 3D cabinet in place, move the camera from the front to the side, and render again. The new image shows the surfaces visible from the side. We do not need to rebuild the mesh for that camera movement. This is what the mesh contributes: the cabinet’s surfaces in 3D . The camera chooses the view, and the renderer calculates the picture. More on rendering [ 3 ] . Renderers can also make pictures from other representations. For 3D Gaussians , the renderer blends the blobs’ projected colors. For a NeRF radiance field , it asks a network about locations along each line of sight. Section 2.5 shows Gaussian projection and blending; Section 2.6 follows a ray through a radiance field.

title: Rendering Gaussians: projection, videos, and opacity
text: 2.5.1 Gaussian rendering: project and blend Start with the fixed 3D blobs introduced in Section 2.3.1 . A camera determines where their colors land in the picture. How do the 3D blobs become an image? A Gaussian renderer projects each 3D blob onto the flat image as a soft oval mark. Where marks overlap, it combines their colors, taking account of which blob is nearer the camera. Placing and blending these projected marks is called splatting . Original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) project [ 1 ] . Watch the 3D setup become a 2D view The image plane is a flat rectangle where we draw the camera’s picture. In this diagram it sits in front of the camera. Seen from its edge, that rectangle looks like a line; the image still has width and height. Open the projection video . 0:00 · The setup 0:06 · Project the blobs 0:16 · Look from the edge 0:26 · Face the image 0:36 · Move the camera First, we rotate our view of the diagram to see the image plane from the side and front. In the last part, the camera itself moves while the two 3D blobs stay in place. The picture on the right shows exactly what that camera renders. The outlined shapes help us see the blobs in 3D. Their rendered marks have soft edges because a Gaussian fades outward. Download the video In the last part, watch the gold mark move behind the blue one, then separate again. The 3D blobs have not moved: the camera now sees them along different lines of sight. Their marks are calculated again for each new camera position. This is how the same 3D scene can produce different 2D pictures. For implementation details, see how gsplat uses the camera and Gaussian shapes to calculate these images [ 2 ] . Now try a whole cabinet The same idea works with many blobs. Here, blue blobs form the drawer, gold blobs form the door, and teal blobs form the cabinet body. First we enlarge one drawer blob; then we follow the cabinet’s colors onto the image plane and move the camera. Open the cabinet video . 0:00 · The cabinet 0:10 · One blob, enlarged 0:24 · Project onto the image 0:38 · Move the camera 0:56 · Compare three views The outlined shapes make the individual blobs visible. The camera picture blends their soft marks together. The cabinet stays still throughout; only the camera moves. This is a deliberately simple teaching model we built, not a reconstruction trained from photographs. Download the cabinet video What does changing opacity actually change? Several blobs can cover the same spot in the camera’s picture. We need one final color at that spot. Opacity decides how strongly the front blob contributes and how much of the color behind it can still show through. In the cabinet video, overlapping blue marks combine to form the drawer’s picture. Opacity is part of that blending step. It does not add paint or a texture to a mesh. Try a blue mark in front of a gold mark. Move the slider and watch how much gold remains visible. The gold stays at 80% opacity; only the blue changes. Two soft projected ellipses overlap at a marked pixel, with the blue contribution in front of the gold One pixel The marked pixel receives color from both overlapping blobs. Blue opacity at the marked pixel 25% Try 25% Try 85% The resulting pixel 25% blue + 60% gold + 15% white background. Blue uses 25% of the pixel’s weight. Gold gets 80% of the remaining 75%: 60%. The background gets the last 15%. Low blue opacity: more gold shows through. High blue opacity: the picture becomes mostly blue at the marked spot. Neither blob has moved; we have changed how their colors combine. The calculation follows one pixel. Across the whole picture, each mark fades toward its edges, and many marks overlap to make the cabinet’s surfaces look continuous. The 3DGS paper gives the projection and blending equations. Many blobs overlap. Their colors build up, so 25% per blob does not mean that the whole cabinet is only 25% opaque. At 0%, none of the blobs contributes color and only the white background remains.

title: 2.6 Radiance fields: rendering with NeRF
text: 2.6 Radiance fields: rendering with NeRF B. Rendering To draw the cabinet, choose a camera and query color and density along its lines of sight. Follow one ray through P1, P2, and P3, then repeat the calculation to form the whole image. Radiance field: Representation · 2.3.2 · Rendering · 2.6 · Reconstruction with NeRF · 2.9

title: Rendering a radiance field
text: 2.6.1 Rendering a radiance field For a radiance field, begin with one image pixel. The camera defines a line of sight through that pixel into the scene. The renderer samples locations along that line and asks the field for color and density there. Along a line toward the drawer, empty air contributes little. Locations near the blue front panel contribute blue and reduce the contribution from behind. Combining the answers produces the pixel’s color. Repeating this across the image produces a view of the cabinet. Here we use the NeRF example introduced in Section 2.3.2 . The network supplies color and density; the renderer supplies the sample locations and combines the answers. Workflow Query a radiance field 01 One query 3D position + viewing direction 02 NeRF network Evaluates the field 03 Two answers Color + density The network’s saved numerical settings are called weights . They determine its answers. During this rendering step, we keep those settings fixed and query the network at different positions.

title: How the renderer generates 3D positions and viewing directions from a pixel
text: 2.6.2 Generate the 3D positions from a camera pixel Start with the camera’s position, orientation, and lens parameters . A virtual camera can supply these settings directly. When matching a photograph, COLMAP [ 1 ] can estimate them, as described in Section 2.7.3 . In either case, the renderer uses the camera settings to calculate sample positions and viewing directions: It selects a pixel in the image to be rendered. It uses the camera position, orientation, and lens parameters to calculate the pixel’s ray : a line of sight extending into the scene. It samples several distances along that ray. Each distance gives a 3D sample position. It sends each position and the ray’s direction to the network. Points on the same ray share the same direction. P1–P3 are sample locations along the ray. The network is queried at these locations before any surface has been identified there. A small coordinate example Here, X points right, Y points toward the cabinet, and Z points up. Coordinates are in meters. The camera is at (0, −3, 0.64) . The selected ray points straight along +Y, so its direction is (0, 1, 0) . Sample Distance from camera 3D position sent to the network P1 1 m (0, −2, 0.64) P2 2 m (0, −1, 0.64) P3 2.54 m (0, −0.46, 0.64) For P2, start at the camera and move 2 m along +Y: the Y coordinate changes from −3 to −1. X and Z stay the same. Other pixels generally produce rays pointing in different directions. In practice, the renderer uses many samples, not just these three. Each sampled 3D position, together with the ray’s viewing direction, forms an input to the NeRF neural network. For P2, the input is position (0, −1, 0.64) and direction (0, 1, 0) . The network predicts a color and density for each sample. Section 2.6.3 explains how the renderer combines these predictions along the ray to produce one pixel’s color.

title: How NeRF renders cabinet samples into one pixel and then an image
text: 2.6.3 From network outputs to the selected pixel Section 2.6.2 calculated P1, P2, and P3 along the ray for one selected image pixel. Each position and the shared viewing direction are supplied as input to the same NeRF network. The network uses its current weights to calculate a color and density for each sample as output . For example, a prediction at P3, near the blue drawer front, could be: Workflow One query near the drawer front 01 P3 input Position: (0, −0.46, 0.64) Direction: (0, 1, 0) 02 NeRF network Evaluates this input 03 P3 output Color: blue Density: high These outputs describe individual samples. The renderer still needs to combine them into one color for the original selected pixel . The diagram continues with the same camera, ray, and sample positions: P1–P3 keep the positions defined in Section 2.6.2. The marked pixel on the right is the pixel whose ray supplied those positions. A prediction that represents this cabinet well assigns low density to the air and blue color with high density near the drawer front: P1 · air Low density gives this sample little influence on the pixel’s color. P2 · air Low density again: most of the view continues toward the drawer. P3 · drawer Blue color and high density: samples around the front panel supply most of the pixel’s color and reduce the contribution from farther behind. The renderer combines the sample colors from near to far. Density and the distance represented by each sample determine how strongly it contributes and how much of the view passes through to later samples. This calculation is called volume rendering . It uses many samples along the ray; P1–P3 are three labeled locations within that process. Rendering details in the paper. [ 2 ] The combined color is written into the original selected pixel. In this example, the drawer front makes that pixel blue. From one pixel to a complete cabinet image The renderer repeats the same calculation for every pixel, using a different ray for each one. The result is an ordinary 2D color image , like this cabinet view: Complete rendered view from the same camera. One ray gives one pixel. The ray through P1–P3 gives the blue pixel discussed above. All the rays give the whole picture. Rays through the drawer produce blue pixels; rays through the door produce gold pixels; rays through the body produce teal pixels. Rays that pass through empty space leave the white background visible. Color and density work together. Color supplies the possible colors along a ray. Density helps determine how much each sample contributes and how much is hidden behind it. After combining them, the finished pixel contains a single color. This completes one render: the field and camera have produced a 2D image. During reconstruction, the same calculation becomes part of a training loop. Section 2.9.3 compares the rendered pixels with a photograph and updates the network.

title: 2.7 Reconstruction: cameras, points, and meshes
text: 2.7 Reconstruction: cameras, points, and meshes C. Reconstruction and generation · COLMAP, DUSt3R, and VGGT Reconstruction estimates a 3D description from photographs. Given overlapping views of the same cabinet, estimate its shape and where the cameras were when the photographs were taken. Workflow From photographs to cameras and geometry 01 2D photographs Several views of the cabinet 02 Choose a method COLMAP, DUSt3R, or VGGT 03 Cameras + 3D geometry Camera settings + surface positions Each complete workflow can provide camera estimates and 3D surface positions . The methods differ in how they obtain these estimates and whether the geometry is represented by sparse points, dense pointmaps, or depth maps. Section 2.4 supplies a scene and camera to make a picture. Here, the pictures are the evidence used to estimate those unknowns. A photograph does not uniquely determine the hidden surfaces, so reconstruction gives an estimate rather than an exact reversal. Inverse rendering describes inferring scene properties from images, often including shape, materials, and lighting. One example recovers all three together. [ 1 ] This section focuses on camera and geometry reconstruction . COLMAP [ 2 ] finds the same details in different photographs, then uses their image positions to estimate cameras and 3D points. DUSt3R [ 3 ] predicts 3D points from image pairs and aligns the pair results. VGGT [ 4 ] jointly processes images to predict cameras and geometry. These are three alternative methods for estimating the photographed scene.

title: Reconstruction and generation: the workflow
text: 2.7.1 Reconstruction and generation: the workflow Where the methods fit Reconstruction uses observations to estimate the scene that was photographed. Generation uses a pretrained model to propose an asset from an image or prompt. Both can produce data in the representations introduced earlier; which output is available depends on the method. Workflow Create 3D data, then render a view Follow either creation route, then use the renderer for its output. Reconstruction Generation 01 Input Reconstruction Cabinet photographs Overlapping views of the same scene. Generation An image or a prompt A condition for a pretrained generator. 02 Method Reconstruction Recover the scene COLMAP, DUSt3R, or VGGT estimates cameras and geometry. Further routes include surface meshes, 3DGS, and NeRF. Generation Propose an asset A generator such as TRELLIS uses prior training to create a supported 3D output. 3D representation For example: points, a mesh, Gaussians, or a field. 01 Renderer + virtual camera Calculate a picture from the chosen viewpoint. 02 2D image A view of the cabinet. During 3DGS / NeRF fitting: render → compare with the input photographs → update the 3D representation → render again. A method can support several output representations. During 3DGS or NeRF fitting, image comparison updates the representation; after fitting, rendering makes new views. COLMAP, DUSt3R, and VGGT offer different routes to camera and geometry estimates. Those geometry estimates are already reconstruction results. With appropriate preparation, they can support surface reconstruction, Gaussian fitting, or NeRF training. The downstream method determines which data and file formats we need. TRELLIS illustrates a pretrained generation route in Section 2.10 . Use rendering to check an estimate In 3DGS and NeRF, rendering checks how well the current 3D description explains the photographs. Workflow Check a 3D estimate 01 Estimate 3D Propose a cabinet representation from its photographs. 02 Render and compare Draw that representation from the photograph’s camera and compare the two images. Adjust the 3D estimate using the image differences, then render and compare again. If the rendered handle appears in the wrong place, the 3D estimate may need to change. The original 3DGS and NeRF methods repeat this comparison across several camera views. Adjusting a representation to match the observed images is called fitting . The photographs are the evidence; the 3D representation is what we adjust. Rendering is the check that connects them: it lets us compare a picture made from the estimate with an actual input picture.

title: What information do we need?
text: 2.7.2 What information do we need? Keep the cabinet, door, and drawer still while photographing from different positions. The images are the observations we want the reconstruction to explain. Camera parameters Where was the camera, which way did it point, and what were its lens settings for each image? These determine the line of sight for each pixel. Geometry estimates Where might the cabinet’s surfaces be in 3D? Depth estimates and 3D points provide information about their locations. Each photograph has a camera viewpoint. Camera information can be supplied when known or estimated during reconstruction. The following examples show how COLMAP, DUSt3R, and VGGT obtain this information. DUSt3R and VGGT use pretrained models to predict geometry for a new scene. When camera positions and settings are already known, we can supply those values directly.

title: COLMAP: match details across views
text: 2.7.3 COLMAP: match details across views COLMAP computes a reconstruction from matching details in the current photographs. For the cabinet, it finds corners and handle details that appear in several views. Their positions in the images provide geometric relationships that COLMAP uses to calculate where the cameras were and where those details lie in 3D. It carries out this calculation for each new set of photographs. Follow the drawer corner marked A: View 1 View 2 View 3 1. Find the same detail in different photos A marks the same cabinet corner in all three views. Its pixel position changes from one picture to another. A match records that two image locations show the same physical detail. COLMAP compares distinctive small image patches to find many such correspondences. Each line connects two observations of one point. The script marks known correspondences to illustrate matching; real photographs supply many more distinctive details. 2. Estimate where the cameras were The image positions of many matched points constrain how the views relate to one another. COLMAP uses these relationships to estimate the cameras’ relative positions and viewing directions. Lens information is supplied when available or estimated as part of the reconstruction. Many matches work together to determine a consistent arrangement. 3. Locate the matched points in 3D With estimated cameras, the pixel marked A in each photo defines a line of sight into the scene. COLMAP estimates A’s 3D position where these lines agree most closely. Repeating this for other matches produces a collection of surface points. This step is called triangulation . Locate one point. Each view gives a line of sight toward A. Combining views estimates its depth. Repeat for many details. The result is sparse: scattered points, with gaps between them. 4. Check the estimates against the photographs COLMAP projects each estimated 3D point back into its photographs. The projected A should land on the observed A. It refines the camera and point estimates to reduce these image-position differences. As more photographs are added, the reconstruction grows and is refined again. This camera-and-point reconstruction is called Structure from Motion (SfM) . The result is camera parameters plus a sparse point cloud : sampled locations on recognizable details. Textured areas often supply more matches than plain panels. COLMAP’s illustrated workflow. Keep the photographs together with these camera and point estimates. They can be prepared for 3DGS or NeRF, as described in Section 2.7.6 . COLMAP’s dense reconstruction tools can instead continue toward depth maps and denser surfaces, as described in Section 2.7.7 .

title: DUSt3R: from image pixels to 3D points
text: 2.7.4 DUSt3R: from image pixels to 3D points DUSt3R is a pretrained model that predicts where photographed surfaces lie in 3D. Its starting inputs are RGB images with overlapping views. For this cabinet, we use left, front, and right views while the drawer and door remain still. The model predicts geometry from image pairs; camera information can then be recovered from those predictions. DUSt3R paper. Left view Front view Right view Scripted illustrations using the book’s shared cabinet. These views stand in for photographs; the point and alignment diagrams below explain the workflow. See the official DUSt3R demo for learned-model results. Predict positions from an image pair Start with the left and front images. DUSt3R processes them together and produces a pointmap for each image . A pointmap follows the image’s rows and columns, but each entry holds three numbers, (X, Y, Z) : the predicted spatial position of the surface seen at that pixel. Both pointmaps from this pair use the same coordinate frame, anchored to the first camera. Image-pair inputs and outputs. Pointmap and point cloud: the same positions, organized differently Follow pixel A near the drawer’s upper-left corner. Its row and column identify a place in the photograph. The corresponding pointmap entry stores a position in 3D. Place that position in a 3D viewer, then repeat for the other entries: the points trace the cabinet’s visible surfaces. 1. Locate an image pixel. The row and column tell us where A is in the picture. 2. Read its pointmap entry. The matching grid cell holds A’s 3D coordinates. The numbers shown are illustrative. 3. View the positions as a cloud. A appears among points on the cabinet. This view uses the same coordinates, seen from another angle. Two organizations of 3D positions Description Pointmap Point cloud How it is organized An image-shaped grid. Each pixel address leads to an XYZ position. A collection of XYZ positions, often with colors or other attributes. For the cabinet Look up pixel A to find its predicted surface position. View points across the drawer, handle, and panels together in 3D. Turning a pointmap into a point cloud keeps the 3D coordinates and changes how we organize or display them. Colors can be copied from the corresponding image pixels. A cloud may also retain the original pixel addresses as extra information. The dots above are a subset of the visible surface samples, spaced out for clarity. Align several image pairs With three photographs, we can process Left + Front and Front + Right . Each pair produces two pointmaps in its own shared frame. To combine the pair results, we need one coordinate system for the whole cabinet. The front image occurs in both pairs. Its pixels therefore connect two predictions of the same surfaces. Global alignment adjusts the pair results and shared geometry so that these overlapping observations agree as closely as possible. Position, orientation, and relative scale are brought into agreement. For example, the two estimates of the drawer corner A should meet in the combined reconstruction. Multi-view alignment. Before alignment. Placing the pair results together without reconciling their frames gives offset surfaces and two locations for A. After alignment. Overlapping surfaces agree; the two pairs also contribute views of different sides. Blue and gold identify the two image pairs. The script deliberately offsets one point set and aligns it using known shared points. This illustrates the purpose of alignment; actual DUSt3R estimates can retain errors. Workflow DUSt3R: predict, then align 01 Overlapping photos Form image pairs 02 DUSt3R predictions Two pointmaps per pair 03 Align pair results One shared reconstruction Keep the reconstruction The aligned positions give a point-cloud reconstruction to inspect. The DUSt3R workflow can also recover camera poses, focal lengths, and depth maps. Keep the original images with these estimates. Building connected surfaces is a further step, described in Section 2.7.7 ; Gaussian or NeRF fitting requires the data preparation described in Section 2.7.6 . The official example shows how to retrieve the cameras and points. For more on confidence, alignment, and scale, see the DUSt3R paper and official implementation .

title: VGGT: predict cameras and geometry
text: 2.7.5 VGGT: predict cameras and geometry VGGT (Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer) uses a pretrained neural network to predict cameras and geometry directly from images . During pretraining, the network learned from many scenes how image information relates to camera viewpoints and 3D surfaces. Its design and training give it specific outputs: camera parameters, depth maps, pointmaps, and tracks for selected image points. VGGT project. For this cabinet, we load the trained model and provide the left, front, and right photographs together. The model uses its learned settings to predict the camera information and visible surface geometry for this cabinet. Those settings stay fixed while it makes the predictions; the same trained model can then process photographs of another object. This use of a trained model is called inference . VGGT accepts one or multiple images; this example uses three overlapping views. Official inference example. These three images show the same stationary cabinet. A marks the same drawer corner in each view. VGGT can also track a selected image point: give it A’s pixel location in one image, and it predicts where that detail appears in the other views. The cabinet images and output diagrams below are script-generated teaching illustrations. They explain the quantities VGGT predicts. See the VGGT project for results produced by the trained model. VGGT jointly processes the supplied views and directly predicts cameras and geometry. Its pointmaps use the same pixel-to-3D organization introduced in the DUSt3R example . DUSt3R’s workflow builds the multi-view result from pair predictions and alignment; VGGT provides a joint prediction from the image set, with optional later refinement. Workflow VGGT: predict cameras and geometry 01 Input Cabinet images 02 VGGT A pretrained geometry model 03 Outputs Cameras + depth / 3D points Camera parameters. Where each image was taken, which way the camera faced, and its lens settings. These let us place virtual cameras at the estimated viewpoints. A depth map for each image. Each pixel holds how far its surface lies along the camera’s viewing direction. The colors here show depth. Combining depth with camera information locates the surface in 3D. Pointmaps, viewed as a point cloud. Each image pixel has a predicted 3D position. Gathering those positions shows the cabinet’s panels and handles together in space. The depth and point predictions already describe geometry. Displaying the predicted surface points in a 3D viewer gives a point-cloud reconstruction of the cabinet. The official VGGT viewer provides examples of inspecting these results. For the next stages in this book, we keep the photographs and export the estimated cameras and 3D points. VGGT’s export tool writes them in COLMAP’s file format, which reconstruction software can read. To obtain a Gaussian scene, continue with a Gaussian training method. The official VGGT integration passes the images, estimated cameras, and points to gsplat [ 5 ] , a Gaussian rendering and training library. Training then adjusts the Gaussians to match the cabinet photographs. Three methods for the same reconstruction task All three workflows can recover cameras and 3D geometry from photographs. Given the same cabinet views, COLMAP calculates these estimates from matches within the supplied photographs. VGGT applies what its network learned during pretraining to predict them. DUSt3R also uses a pretrained network, with image-pair prediction followed by alignment and camera recovery. Their steps and outputs are: Method Main steps Result at this stage COLMAP: sparse SfM Compute from current photo matches. Match cabinet details across views; use their image positions to estimate cameras and triangulate 3D points, then refine the estimates. Estimated cameras and sparse points. COLMAP’s dense tools can continue from here. DUSt3R Predict with a pretrained model, then align. Predict pointmaps for cabinet image pairs; align the pair results and recover cameras. Dense surface positions, with cameras and depth recoverable through the workflow. VGGT Predict with a pretrained model. Process the cabinet images together using the trained network and directly predict cameras and geometry. Optional refinement can follow. Camera parameters, depth, pointmaps, and tracks for selected image points. Choose one of these reconstruction routes, then prepare its outputs for the next task. The following sections explain how different downstream methods use the cameras and geometry.

title: Where do these outputs go next?
text: 2.7.6 Where do these outputs go next? Section 2.7 prepares photographs, camera parameters, and initial geometry estimates. Sections 2.8 and 2.9 use that preparation in two alternative reconstruction methods: fitting 3D Gaussians or training a NeRF network. Each method builds a 3D representation whose rendered views match the cabinet photographs. Both methods repeatedly use 3D → 2D rendering , introduced in Section 2.4 : render the current representation, compare it with a photograph from the same camera, and use the differences to improve the representation. Continue with 3DGS Inputs: photographs, camera parameters, and estimated 3D points. Use estimated 3D points as starting locations for Gaussians. Use each camera to render the current Gaussians from its photograph’s viewpoint. Compare with that photograph and adjust the Gaussians. Saved result: the fitted Gaussian parameters. Follow the cabinet in Section 2.8 Continue with NeRF Inputs: photographs and camera parameters. Use each camera to construct rays through image pixels. Sample positions along those rays and query a network for color and density. Render pixels, compare with the photographs, and adjust the network. Saved result: a trained network that describes the cabinet. Follow the cabinet in Section 2.9 The 3D points play different roles. In the 3DGS route, estimated surface points provide starting locations for blobs. In the original NeRF route, the renderer chooses query locations along camera rays, including in empty space. Each query position and viewing direction is sent to the NeRF network; the samples span the ray rather than just the estimated surfaces. The 3DGS and NeRF worked examples use COLMAP-style camera preparation. The VGGT export offers another way to supply camera and point estimates; the later rendering and fitting stages still need to be carried out. DUSt3R estimates can serve a similar preparation role when converted for the chosen implementation. This involves checking camera conventions, image sizes, scene scale, and file format. The pointmap or point cloud is a geometry result; fitting a Gaussian scene or NeRF is a separate stage. A mesh is another possible reconstruction output. A workflow can estimate denser geometry and build connected surfaces from it; COLMAP’s dense reconstruction tools [ 6 ] support that route. Further details: original 3DGS inputs [ 7 ] and original NeRF camera preparation [ 8 ] .

title: Reconstruct a mesh from cabinet photographs
text: 2.7.7 From points to a mesh Mesh: Representation · 2.2 · Rendering · 2.4 · Reconstruction · 2.7.7 To obtain a mesh of the photographed cabinet , we need surface faces as well as 3D positions. This route builds on the cameras and geometry estimated earlier: Prepare dense surface points. Starting from sparse COLMAP output, estimate depth across the photographs and combine the results into a dense point cloud. With DUSt3R or VGGT, collect reliable positions from the predicted pointmaps in a shared coordinate frame. These routes supply samples on the cabinet’s panels and handle. Estimate a surface from those points. A surface-reconstruction algorithm uses the samples to decide where a continuous surface should lie. It may also use estimates of which way the surface faces. It creates connected faces that follow that surface. Save and inspect the mesh. The result contains vertices and faces, as introduced in Section 2.2 . Check that the panel shapes, handle, and spaces around moving parts have been captured. For example, the dense points may mark many locations on the drawer front. The mesh adds surface patches covering the panel between those locations. Around the handle, the reconstructed surface should follow the grip and preserve the opening behind it. COLMAP’s dense route: photographs + cameras → depth estimates → dense 3D points → a surface mesh. Predicted pointmaps offer another source of dense points for surface reconstruction. The Gaussian and NeRF routes in Sections 2.8 and 2.9 fit blobs or a network to the photographs. Photo coverage and the surface-reconstruction method affect which details can be recovered. COLMAP’s dense reconstruction tools and Open3D’s surface-reconstruction examples [ 9 ] show implementations of this route.

title: 2.8 Gaussians: reconstruction with 3DGS and 2DGS
text: 2.8 Gaussians: reconstruction with 3DGS and 2DGS C. Reconstruction and generation · 3DGS and 2DGS 3DGS and 2DGS are two ways to reconstruct the same cabinet from photographs. Both first fit a 3D representation to multiple views, then use the saved result and a virtual camera to render new views. Choose either method for a reconstruction. To compare them, run each on the same prepared photographs and cameras, producing two separate results. Each result uses its corresponding renderer. 3D Gaussians: Representation · 2.3.1 · Rendering · 2.5 · Reconstruction with 3DGS · 2.8

title: 3DGS and 2DGS: the shared task and different emphasis
text: The same photographs, two reconstruction methods Original 3DGS focuses on making accurate-looking views of the scene. Its training adjusts soft 3D ellipsoids until their rendered pictures resemble the photographs. 2DGS also fits the pictures, while explicitly encouraging a consistent surface. It uses flat Gaussian disks and adds training constraints on where the surface lies and which way it faces. See the 3DGS [ 1 ] and 2DGS [ 2 ] projects. For the blue drawer front, image quality means that the blue panel and handle look right in a rendered picture. Surface quality means that the recovered panel lies in the right place in 3D, faces the right direction, and forms a coherent surface. These are two ways to evaluate the reconstruction. Workflow One set of cabinet photographs, two routes Each route fits its own representation. The steps line up for comparison. Prepare shared inputs Cabinet photographs, camera parameters, and sparse 3D points. ↗ 3DGS 2DGS 01 Initialize 3DGS Soft ellipsoids Three sizes describe width, height, and thickness. 2DGS Flat Gaussian disks Two sizes describe a plane placed and oriented in 3D. 02 Fit repeatedly 3DGS Render → compare → adjust Use the 3DGS renderer. Compare with the same-camera photograph and adjust using image differences. 2DGS Render → compare → adjust Use the 2DGS renderer. Adjust using image differences and surface constraints for depth and facing direction. 03 Save 3DGS Fitted ellipsoids Store the Gaussians and their learned parameters. 2DGS Fitted disks Store the disks and their learned parameters. 04 Use the result 3DGS Render new views Saved ellipsoids + a new camera + the 3DGS renderer → a 2D color image. 2DGS Two uses of the saved disks New view: new camera + 2DGS renderer → a 2D color image. Optional mesh: render depth maps → combine depth → extract surfaces. Fitting loop: repeat rendering, comparison, and adjustment across the input camera views before saving. Mesh extraction uses the saved 2DGS disks to render depth; new color images are a separate output. A 3DGS mesh requires an additional surface-reconstruction workflow. Read either column from top to bottom. Matching steps line up across the two methods. Gold highlights method-specific details, including 2DGS constraints on surface depth and facing direction. Each fitting loop repeats before its result is saved. The optional mesh branch starts from the saved disks. For a cabinet viewer, both methods can produce new camera views. When recovering panel surfaces and an editable mesh is also a goal, 2DGS provides a workflow designed around that goal. Inspect both the rendered pictures and the recovered geometry for the intended use. The two walkthroughs below use the same five steps: prepare → initialize → render and adjust → save → use .

title: Fit the cabinet Gaussians to photographs
text: The 3DGS fitting loop in pictures This is a teaching diagram. Rendered cabinet views stand in for photographs; the stages below illustrate the process, rather than showing a recorded training run. Initialize the blobs and render a first picture Initial 3D blobs Points now have size, color, and opacity. Their rendered 2D image The drawer and handle look blurry. Reference view The image we want to match. Compare from the same camera position. Otherwise, a difference could simply come from looking at the cabinet from a different angle. Use the image differences to update the blobs Workflow Fit the Gaussian cabinet 01 Render 3D blobs → 2D image 02 Compare Rendered image ↔ photo 03 Update Change the 3D blobs Render again, compare again, update again. The comparison gives an error: how different are the images? The fitting process uses that error to adjust the blobs. For example, several smaller blobs can describe the handle more precisely than one large, blurry blob. Adjust Change position, size, orientation, color, or opacity. Add detail Clone a blob, or split a large one into smaller ones. Remove Discard blobs with very low opacity. These changes happen in 3D , so they affect several camera views. The original 3DGS method alternates parameter updates with adding and removing blobs. Fit across the views, then render a new view A closer match Many overlapping blobs form a clearer cabinet image. A new camera view Render the same 3D blobs from another position. Fitting repeats across the photographs so that one set of 3D blobs explains many views . We save those blobs and can then render new views. This is the purpose of the 3DGS representation ; it does not automatically add a drawer joint or the cabinet’s mass.

title: Reconstruct the cabinet with 3DGS
text: Reconstruct the cabinet with 3DGS Prepare the inputs. Collect overlapping cabinet photographs. Use the COLMAP workflow in Section 2.7.3 [ 3 ] to estimate cameras and sparse 3D points. The points provide starting locations for the Gaussians. Initialize the elements. Place a soft 3D ellipsoid at each starting point. Give it a position, orientation, three sizes, opacity, and appearance. Render, compare, and adjust. Render from a training photograph’s camera and compare the pixels. Adjust the ellipsoids to reduce the image differences, repeating across the views. The method can also add, split, or remove elements. At the blue drawer, the fit is guided by how well the rendered panel and handle match the photographs. Save the fitted representation. Keep the ellipsoids’ positions, orientations, sizes, opacity, and appearance. Together they describe this cabinet in 3D. Use the result. Give the saved ellipsoids and a new virtual camera to a 3DGS renderer to make another image. Surface reconstruction is an additional operation when a mesh is needed. Section 2.5.1 explains the rendering operation used in Step 3: project the ellipsoids into soft image marks and blend them. The original paper explains the updates. The VGGT export in Section 2.7.5 provides another source of cameras and starting points for a supported Gaussian training pipeline.

title: 2DGS: reconstruct with surface Gaussians
text: 2DGS: reconstruct with surface Gaussians 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) reconstructs a scene using oriented Gaussian disks. For the cabinet, these disks can follow the drawer front, side panels, and top. It fits them to photographs while also encouraging a coherent surface. 2DGS project. What does “2D” describe? Both methods describe a scene in 3D and render 2D images. Here, “2D” and “3D” describe the dimensions of one Gaussian element : 3DGS: a soft volume. Each element has three size parameters, shown here as width, height, and thickness. Its position and orientation place that volume in 3D. 2DGS: a soft surface patch. Each element has two sizes within its plane and zero thickness through it. Its center still has three coordinates, and its orientation determines which way the plane faces. Both elements store opacity and appearance, with influence fading away from the center. The outlines are shape guides; the edge-on line makes the disk’s plane visible. A 3D Gaussian can also become very flat during fitting. 2DGS explicitly uses a plane and a renderer designed for it. Arrange the elements around the same cabinet A disk on the drawer front faces forward; one on the side faces sideways; one on top faces upward. Many such patches describe a 3D object. The front and back of a thick panel can be represented by separate sets of surface patches. 3D Gaussian elements. The guides show their extent through space. 2D Gaussian elements. Each disk lies in its own oriented plane. Scripted illustrations with the same cabinet, camera, and 29 selected centers. The pale solid cabinet provides context; the colored guides show individual elements. A fitted reconstruction uses many more elements. These diagrams illustrate their structure; the authors’ results show reconstruction quality. What does improving the drawer surface mean? Both methods adjust their elements to make the blue drawer look right in the photographs. 2DGS also encourages the patches to describe one coherent panel in 3D. Along a view of the drawer front, its constraints encourage the visible contributions to gather near one surface depth. They also encourage the disks to face in directions that agree with the reconstructed panel’s shape. This helps when recovering the panel’s surface and extracting a mesh. The image fit, disk geometry, and surface constraints work together. Their technical names and equations are in the paper’s depth-distortion and normal-consistency description . Reconstruct the cabinet with 2DGS Prepare the inputs. Collect overlapping cabinet photographs. Use the same COLMAP workflow in Section 2.7.3 to estimate cameras and sparse 3D points. The official 2DGS implementation accepts this preparation. Initialize the elements. Place a soft disk at each starting point. Give it a position, orientation, two sizes within its plane, opacity, and appearance. Render, compare, and adjust. Render from a training photograph’s camera and compare the pixels. Adjust the disks using both image differences and the surface constraints above, repeating across the views. The method can also add, split, or remove elements. At the blue drawer, both its photographed appearance and the consistency of its recovered panel guide the fit. Save the fitted representation. Keep the disks’ positions, orientations, sizes, opacity, and appearance. Together they describe this cabinet in 3D. Use the result. Give the saved disks and a new virtual camera to a 2DGS renderer to make another image. For a mesh, use the supplied depth-fusion and surface-extraction workflow described below. In Step 3, the 2DGS renderer calculates where each pixel’s camera ray meets a disk’s plane, then blends the disks’ contributions into the pixel. This uses the plane’s location and orientation in 3D. See the rendering description and official training implementation . A mesh is an additional output. The provided extraction workflow renders depth maps from several cameras. It combines those depth observations—a step called depth fusion —then extracts connected surface faces. The resulting mesh can be inspected in a mesh editor: check the cabinet panels and the gap behind the handle. See the official mesh-extraction workflow and rendering and geometry examples . To describe how the recovered object’s parts move, a mesh can continue into Articulate AnyMesh in Section 3.6 [ 4 ] . Its project demonstrates this route from a 2DGS surface mesh to an articulated URDF.

title: 2.9 Radiance fields: reconstruction with NeRF
text: 2.9 Radiance fields: reconstruction with NeRF C. Reconstruction and generation · Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) First, train: use multiple views of the cabinet and their camera information to train a network representing the cabinet in 3D. Repeatedly render images, compare with the photographs, and update the network. Then, render: use the saved network and a new virtual camera position and settings to produce another view of the same cabinet. No photograph from that new angle is needed. Radiance field: Representation · 2.3.2 · Rendering · 2.6 · Reconstruction with NeRF · 2.9

title: NeRF: photograph one cabinet
text: 2.9.1 Photograph the cabinet Take overlapping photographs from several positions. Keep the cabinet, drawer, and door still. Each photograph shows the same scene from a different viewpoint. Photo 1 · from the left Photo 2 · from the front Photo 3 · from the right The original NeRF [ 1 ] is trained separately for each scene. Photographs of this cabinet provide the training images: the network learns a description of this particular cabinet from those views. The three views illustrate the image collection step. Reconstruction may use many more photographs to cover the scene.

title: Prepare NeRF inputs: images and camera parameters
text: 2.9.2 Prepare images and camera parameters The NeRF training pipeline takes the scene’s images and each image’s camera position, orientation, and lens parameters as input. Position specifies where the camera was; orientation specifies which way it pointed. Lens parameters, such as focal length, determine how the scene projects onto the image. Each cabinet image is associated with the camera position and orientation used to capture that view. Use the camera estimates from Section 2.7 Section 2.7.3 explains how COLMAP [ 2 ] estimates cameras from the cabinet photographs. Section 2.7.5 introduces VGGT’s camera and geometry predictions [ 3 ] . Either route must supply camera data in the form expected by the chosen NeRF implementation. In the workflow illustrated here, COLMAP supplies the camera estimates. Keep each photograph paired with its camera position, orientation, and lens parameters. The original NeRF code describes this preparation. Workflow From prepared cameras to field queries 01 Prepared inputs Cabinet photos + camera parameters 02 NeRF renderer Rays + sampled 3D positions 03 NeRF network Color + density per sample NeRF uses the same photographs and camera estimates through a separate reconstruction route. The 3DGS and NeRF routes branch after input preparation. In NeRF, the renderer calculates the sample positions sent to the network. Start with a NeRF network whose weights have not yet been fitted to this cabinet. Rendering its current predictions gives images that can be compared with the photographs. Training adjusts the weights to reduce the differences. NeRF training sequence Estimate the cameras. COLMAP processes the cabinet photographs and estimates the camera parameters associated with each image. Calculate rays and sample positions. NeRF’s renderer uses the camera parameters to construct a ray through a selected pixel, then samples 3D positions along that ray. Query the neural network. Each sample position and its viewing direction enter the network, which predicts a color and density. Render and compare. The renderer combines those predictions into a pixel color and compares it with the corresponding pixel in the cabinet photograph. Update the network. The training algorithm adjusts the network’s numerical settings, called weights, to reduce the color error. Steps 2–5 repeat across pixels and camera views. COLMAP supplies camera estimates during data preparation. The repeated training loop updates the NeRF network . The photographs provide target colors; the renderer calculates the positions and directions sent to the network. Section 2.6.2 illustrates the ray and sample positions for one cabinet pixel.

title: The complete NeRF training loop: compare cabinet images and update weights
text: 2.9.3 Compare with the photograph, then learn In this example, the predicted drawer is gray, but the reference image shows blue. Both images use the same camera, so corresponding pixel colors can be compared directly. Current prediction The drawer color and edges are wrong. Photograph to match The reference drawer is blue. Workflow Fit the field to the photographs 01 Render a prediction. Generate rays, query the network, and combine its answers. 02 Measure the error. Compare the predicted colors with the corresponding photo pixels. 03 Adjust the network’s weights. The training algorithm calculates changes intended to reduce that error. 04 Repeat with more pixels and views. Render again with the updated network and compare again. Repeat across the photographed camera views, updating the network’s weights. The photographs provide target pixel colors, without labeling the density at P3 or the drawer’s surface position. Views from other cameras help constrain the 3D arrangement: a misplaced panel might match one view but appear in the wrong place in another. Rendering and comparison are repeated throughout training. As the network’s weights change to reduce image errors, its 3D description improves. One network is trained to account for the cabinet across the input views. The original training procedure.

title: Save the trained NeRF and render another view of the same cabinet
text: 2.9.4 Save the trained NeRF and render another view Training is complete; save the network’s learned weights. These weights are the stored 3D description of this cabinet. To make another picture, load that same network and choose a new virtual camera. Stage Input Result Train the NeRF Cabinet photographs + their camera parameters A trained network representing the cabinet in 3D Render a view The trained network + a chosen virtual camera A 2D image of the same cabinet from that camera One saved scene, many camera views Workflow Render a new view 01 Saved NeRF + new camera Keep the learned weights fixed 02 Render Calculate rays, query color and density, combine the answers 03 New 2D view A picture of the same cabinet For a right-side view, place the virtual camera on the right and render. For a higher view, move it upward and render again. Every view is calculated directly from the same saved network. Only the camera and the resulting queries change. This uses the rendering calculation in Section 2.6.3 . Rendering a viewpoint absent from the training photographs is called novel-view synthesis. This is a main use of NeRF: showing the same scene from another viewpoint. Camera estimation and network training belong to the earlier reconstruction stage; here, the saved result is ready to render. NeRF project and examples. Inspect the 3D answers Samples on several slices reveal the panels. These dots visualize answers; they are not what a NeRF stores. Same cabinet, another viewpoint The camera moves; the saved 3D representation stays the same. An unseen back or interior can still be wrong. Good-looking views do not guarantee accurate hidden geometry, moving joints, or mass. The stored scene differs from 3DGS : 3DGS adjusts a set of blobs; NeRF adjusts a network. Both use rendered images to check a 3D representation against photographs.
