title: 2.10 Generation: TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D
text: 2.10 Generation: TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D C. Reconstruction and generation · Pretrained 3D generators A pretrained 3D generator offers another route to a 3D asset, the object’s digital model. Give the system a cabinet image, and it uses knowledge learned from many objects to propose the cabinet’s shape and appearance in 3D. We follow two examples: TRELLIS [ 1 ] creates a shared 3D description that can be decoded into several representations; Hunyuan3D 2.0 [ 2 ] creates a mesh, then generates its texture. Both use the shape, appearance, and rendering concepts from Parts A and B. The routes in 2.8 and 2.9 fit a cabinet’s representation to photographs of that scene. Here, pretrained systems use an input image to guide the creation of a new asset. The examples below refer to the original TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D 2.0 releases.

title: TRELLIS: generate a 3D asset from one image
text: 2.10.1 TRELLIS: generate a 3D asset from one image TRELLIS is the first generator we examine. Its image-based model takes a cabinet picture and uses knowledge learned during prior training to propose the cabinet’s shape and appearance in 3D. The result can be output as a mesh, 3D Gaussians, or a radiance field . TRELLIS project. Suppose the input photograph shows the cabinet’s front. It provides little direct evidence about the back or interior. TRELLIS uses patterns learned during training to propose those unseen regions. The result is a plausible asset; hidden details still need inspection if we want to reproduce a particular real cabinet. TRELLIS creates the asset; its output representation determines how the 3D information is stored. The three options below use the representations introduced in Section 2.1 . Mesh output Vertices and connected faces describe surfaces. Appearance can be supplied with textures and materials. Gaussian output Positions, shapes, opacity, and appearance describe blobs that a Gaussian renderer blends into views. Radiance field output Color and density describe the scene at locations in 3D. To make a picture, provide the field and a virtual camera to a compatible volume renderer . It reads color and density along camera rays and combines them into pixels, as in Section 2.6.3 . For the cabinet, choose a camera on its right to render a right-side view. Keep the field unchanged; choose another camera to make another view. To use a TRELLIS result, choose software that supports its output: a mesh editor or mesh renderer for meshes, a Gaussian viewer or renderer for Gaussians, and a compatible volume renderer for radiance fields. TRELLIS provides a renderer for its own radiance-field output. Its official example uses it to make a video from a sequence of camera views. The field’s saved form can differ from the original NeRF network described in Section 2.9.

title: TRELLIS: choosing an output for the cabinet
text: 2.10.2 TRELLIS: choosing an output for the cabinet Two of TRELLIS’s output options are a mesh and 3D Gaussians. The cabinet illustrations below show what those representations look like and help explain when each is useful. They are rendered from the book’s scripted cabinet; published TRELLIS predictions are available in the authors’ gallery . One cabinet picture A front view is a flat image. It does not show the cabinet’s hidden sides. Mesh representation Connected surfaces describe the shape. Lines reveal the triangular faces. Gaussian representation Projecting and blending the 3D blobs makes this picture. Both representations can show color. The mesh and Gaussian views here share a camera and color scheme. The triangle lines help us inspect the mesh; a renderer can hide those lines and use textures and materials to show its appearance. Using TRELLIS’s mesh output Suppose we want to use the generated cabinet in a robot-grasping experiment. Choosing TRELLIS’s mesh output gives us surface patches to inspect and edit. We can check the handle’s shape and the gap behind it, then prepare shapes for contact. We can also organize its geometry into parts before adding joints and physical properties. Using TRELLIS’s Gaussian output If our immediate goal is to display the asset from new viewpoints, a Gaussian representation supplies colored blobs that can be projected and blended directly. The same rendering operation works for Gaussians produced by TRELLIS or fitted with 3DGS. The choice depends on what we want to do with the result; surface geometry and Gaussian appearance can also be used together. Original 3DGS project [ 3 ] .

title: Hunyuan3D: first shape, then texture
text: 2.10.3 Hunyuan3D: first shape, then texture Hunyuan3D 2.0 separates asset creation into two stages: generate the surface shape, then generate its appearance. Its image-based pipeline takes a reference picture and produces a textured mesh. Official architecture overview. Input: a cabinet picture The picture guides the proposed shape and colors. Stage 1: bare mesh Surfaces define the cabinet’s depth, panels, and raised handles. Stage 2: add appearance The mesh receives color and surface patterns through a texture map. Scripted illustrations of the stages, using the book’s shared cabinet. The gray and colored views have identical geometry; authored surface colors illustrate the appearance stage. Published model results are available in the Hunyuan3D gallery . Shape generation: where are the surfaces? The shape model, Hunyuan3D-DiT , uses the cabinet picture to create a mesh. Its surfaces describe the depth of the body, the front of the drawer, and the handle sticking out. At this stage, we can inspect the cabinet’s shape before adding its colors. Shape-generation method. Texture generation: how do those surfaces look? Hunyuan3D-Paint receives that mesh together with the reference picture and generates its texture. For the cabinet, this supplies colors such as the blue drawer front and gold door, along with surface patterns shown in the picture. The texture is saved as an image whose regions are placed on the corresponding mesh surfaces. Texture-generation method. For the cabinet, the texture supplies the blue paint or wood grain; the mesh supplies the handle’s shape. Paint can also texture a mesh prepared in Blender , so an existing model can enter directly at the appearance stage. The official code example shows the mesh and image passed into the texture pipeline. Use the saved asset The mesh and its texture can be opened in compatible 3D software. Place a virtual camera in the scene to render a front or side view, as in Section 2.4 . Preparing this asset for drawer-opening experiments then involves organizing the movable parts and their joints, introduced in Section 3.2 .

title: Compare the workflows and outputs
text: 2.10.4 Compare the workflows and outputs Suppose we give each system the same picture of a cabinet with a blue drawer and a gold door. Both use knowledge learned during training to propose a 3D cabinet. We can compare the steps that create it and the kind of 3D data we receive . Hunyuan3D: build the shape, then add a texture The first stage creates the cabinet’s mesh: surfaces describe its panels, depth, and raised handles. The second stage uses this mesh and the input picture to generate colors and surface patterns. The result is a mesh with a texture , ready to open in compatible 3D software and render from a chosen camera. TRELLIS: build a shared description, then choose an output TRELLIS first proposes where to place information about the cabinet’s surfaces in 3D space. It then generates a numerical description of the shape and appearance around those locations—for example, the shape of the drawer front and its blue color. This description is an intermediate result used inside the system. TRELLIS can convert that shared description into several output representations : a mesh with connected surfaces, 3D Gaussians made of colored blobs, or a radiance field that supplies color and density. These are the forms introduced in Part A . For example, choose a mesh to edit the handle’s surface in a mesh editor, or Gaussians to view the cabinet with a Gaussian renderer. TRELLIS outputs. Workflow From a cabinet picture Compare what each stage creates and what can be saved. Input: a cabinet picture The same kind of reference is used for both examples. Hunyuan3D 2.0 Original TRELLIS 01 First stage Hunyuan3D 2.0 Create the shape Generate a bare mesh of the cabinet panels and handles. Original TRELLIS Choose 3D locations Choose active locations near the cabinet’s surfaces. 02 Second stage Hunyuan3D 2.0 Add a texture Generate colors and patterns guided by the image. Original TRELLIS Describe shape and appearance Generate local codes around the chosen locations. 03 Output Hunyuan3D 2.0 Textured mesh A surface shape with its appearance. Original TRELLIS Choose a representation Decode the description into a mesh, Gaussians, or a radiance field. The workflows shown here: original TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D 2.0 What to compare Hunyuan3D 2.0 TRELLIS How the cabinet is created Create the surface mesh, then generate its texture. Choose locations in 3D, describe shape and appearance there, then convert that description into an output. What we receive A mesh with a texture. A mesh, 3D Gaussians, or a radiance field. Further reading: internal codes and texture generation TRELLIS terminology. The selected locations are cells in a sparse 3D grid . The numbers generated at each location are feature codes . Locations and codes together form the structured latent representation (SLAT) . A decoder is the learned component that converts this internal description into a particular output representation. The TRELLIS paper explains the two generation stages. Hunyuan3D shape and texture. The shape model generates a compact numerical description that is decoded into a mesh. For texture generation, the pipeline renders geometric information from several viewpoints; Paint uses it with the reference image to generate colored views. Transferring those colors onto a texture map is called texture baking . See the paper’s shape method and texture method . Exporting a textured mesh from TRELLIS. Its GLB export can transfer appearance from the generated Gaussians onto the generated mesh. The official export notes describe this step. For Hunyuan3D, the code examples show how to use the shape and Paint models.

title: 3D software: Blender, Maya, and MeshLab
text: 3D software: Blender, Maya, and MeshLab 3D software lets us create and edit models, make camera images, and work with movement. The mesh is the shape data; the application provides tools for working with it.

title: Blender
text: Blender Blender [ 1 ] is a free, open-source application for creating 3D content. We can build and edit meshes, add materials and lights, animate objects, run physics simulations, and render camera images. For a cabinet, it can handle everything from shaping the drawer to making a video of its movement.

title: Maya
text: Maya Autodesk Maya [ 2 ] is a 3D creation application with tools for modeling, rigging, animation, rendering, and simulation. We can use it to build a cabinet, set up controls for its moving parts, and produce images or animation. The rigging, keyframe, and animation-curve tools illustrated below are available in both Maya and Blender.

title: MeshLab
text: MeshLab MeshLab [ 3 ] focuses on inspecting and processing triangle meshes. We can use it to clean up a reconstructed cabinet, remove stray fragments, and reduce the number of faces. After simplifying a model, check that the handle keeps its shape and the opening behind it remains clear. MeshLab’s role here is to prepare the geometry. For the rigging and keyframe animation shown below, we use Blender or Maya. A mesh cleaned in MeshLab can be exported and opened in either application. The following examples illustrate modeling and rendering , animation , and physics simulation . The screenshots identify the application used; the animation diagrams explain concepts shared by Blender and Maya.

title: Modeling and rendering
text: Modeling and rendering First, build the object’s shape and make a picture of it. The screenshots in this example use Blender . Maya also provides mesh editing, materials, lights, cameras, and rendering; its interface looks different. Example: from a portrait mesh to a picture These Blender screenshots follow a portrait model. The mesh gives it shape, a virtual camera chooses the view, and rendering produces a picture using that view, the materials, and the lighting. 1. Build and inspect the mesh The gray model is made of small, flat faces. Together, they form the head, hat, and other parts. The colored rectangle is a 2D reference image used as a guide while modeling. ⤢ Modeling against a reference. The orange outline marks the selected reference image. ⤢ Inspecting from another angle. The model has depth; the reference remains a flat picture. We can move around the model in Blender’s 3D viewport —the editing area—to inspect its shape. A reference picture helps with modeling; it is not the camera or the finished render. Blender’s reference-image guide explains this setup. 2. Choose the virtual camera’s view Think of placing a camera in front of a sculpture. In Blender, we position a virtual camera, aim it at the model, and choose how much of the scene fits in the frame. This camera defines the view used for the final image. The yellow wireframe below is the camera object in the scene. Each row pairs a camera setup with a preview of the model from that viewpoint. ⤢ Camera position A. An outside view shows where the camera sits relative to the model. ⤢ View A. The eyes and nose are hidden from this angle. ⤢ Camera position B. The camera looks toward the model from another position. ⤢ View B. The eyes and nose are now visible. A different viewpoint reveals different parts of the same model. We can choose another camera view without rebuilding the mesh. The grid and black guide lines in these previews are Blender overlays, not part of the portrait. Workflow Scene, camera, and rendering 01 3D scene Model, materials, and lights. 02 Virtual camera Choose the viewpoint and framing. 03 Render Calculate a 2D picture from that view. 3. Render the surface appearance With the camera set, the renderer calculates the output image. Blender displays it in the Render Result window. ⤢ 3D editing view. The grid helps us navigate around the model. ⤢ Rendered camera view. Blender’s Render Result window shows a 2D picture with lighting and shadows. The editing view and the render above are cropped from the same screenshot. Moving around the editor lets us inspect the object; changing the render camera changes the viewpoint of the output image. ⤢ A colored render of the portrait model. The mesh supplies the shape. Materials give surfaces their appearance, such as a blue hat or a shiny earring. Lighting affects the bright areas and shadows. Rendering calculates the pixels of the camera image. The result is a 2D picture that we can save and share. The editable 3D model remains in the scene, ready to be viewed from another camera angle. For our cabinet, we could import a mesh, look around it, and check whether the handle is a real raised shape. If the handle or drawer tray is missing, we can build it. We can also separate the drawer and door into objects that can be moved independently. To make a picture, we place a camera and lights and choose a renderer. Blender includes Eevee and Cycles . They calculate images using the model’s surfaces and materials. Useful starting points: modeling , materials , and rendering .

title: Animation in both applications
text: Animation in Blender and Maya Blender and Maya provide the rigging, keyframe, and animation-curve tools used in these examples. MeshLab is a tool for processing meshes. It does not offer the rigging and keyframe animation tools used below. Consider an animated arm reaching toward our cabinet, followed by the drawer opening. We first set up controls for the parts, then choose their positions over time. The diagrams illustrate the ideas rather than either application’s interface. 1. Rigging: set up how the parts move The arm’s shape is already modeled. Now we tell the software where its parts can turn and which pieces should move together . We place joints at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist, then connect the visible arm pieces to those joints. We can also add a control that the animator can select and move. This preparation is called rigging . The resulting controls and connections form the rig . Using those controls to arrange the arm is called posing . The picture shows the rig being used after setup. Move the hand control toward the cabinet handle, and the software turns the connected arm joints to reach that position. This is inverse kinematics (IK) . It works within the arm’s reach and the rig’s settings; we can also control which way the elbow bends. See Blender’s IK constraint or Maya’s mechanical-arm example . ⤢ The rig is already set up in both views. Gold circles mark joints, and the dashed box is the hand control. Moving that control changes the pose; it does not apply a physical pulling force. For a character with a flexible surface, skinning connects the mesh to the skeleton so the surface bends with it. A rigid cabinet drawer can simply move as one piece. The cabinet needs a simpler setup than this arm: one control can slide the whole drawer, and another can rotate the door around its hinge. It does not need a human-shaped skeleton. 2. Keyframes: choose when the drawer opens A keyframe records a value at a chosen time. Set the drawer’s opening to 0 cm at 0 seconds and 40 cm at 2 seconds . Either application can calculate the positions between those keys. With constant speed, the drawer is 20 cm open after 1 second. ⤢ The two gold keys are values we choose. The middle position is calculated between them; we do not need to position the drawer separately in every frame. 3. Graph Editor: adjust how the movement feels The Graph Editor displays values over time. Here, the horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is drawer opening. A straight line gives constant speed. A curve that starts and ends gently makes the drawer speed up and then slow down. We can edit the curve while keeping the same start and end positions. Both Blender and Maya provide a Graph Editor. ⤢ The line describes the drawer’s position, not its physical path through the room. Both examples still slide along the same straight rail. These tools let us design a movement . Changing the curve changes the positions the animation follows. Calculating motion from gravity, a pull, or a collision requires a physics setup.

title: Physics simulation example
text: Physics simulation: a box falls onto a shelf Open the lower door of the same cabinet, place a small box above its bottom shelf, and let go. We want gravity to make it fall and contact with the shelf to stop it. Blender and Maya can both run this kind of rigid-body simulation , in which the objects move without changing shape. The example below was calculated in Blender using its rigid-body physics system. The cabinet and box were built by a script, and a fixed camera rendered the calculated positions. Prepare the objects. Give the movable box a mass of 1 kg and a box-shaped collision boundary. Give the cabinet walls and shelf fixed collision shapes. Set the starting conditions. Start the box at rest above the shelf and enable gravity. No keyframes tell it where to go or when to stop. Run the physics calculation. The simulator updates the box’s motion over time. Contact with the shelf prevents it from passing through. Render the result. The camera makes pictures of those computed positions using the scene’s materials and lighting. ⤢ 0 seconds: release. We choose this starting position. ⤢ 0.2 seconds: falling. Gravity changes its speed and position. ⤢ 0.6 seconds: supported. Contact with the shelf stops the fall. The last two positions are simulation outputs. We supplied the starting pose, gravity, and physical settings. With gravity off, this box would remain at rest in the air; without the shelf’s collision shape, it would fall through the visible shelf. Where are these settings in each application? In Blender , use the Rigid Body physics settings: an Active box is moved by the simulation, while Passive cabinet parts stay fixed in this example. In Maya , the Bullet plug-in provides rigid bodies and a solver to calculate their motion. The commands differ, but both need the objects, collision shapes, and physical settings. See Blender’s rigid-body introduction and Maya’s Bullet guide . A rig control sets a pose for animation. A force , such as gravity, changes motion through a physics calculation. Both can be used within either application. For the drawer’s pulling-force examples, see From animation to simulation .

title: A cabinet workflow
text: A cabinet workflow Open the model. Import an existing cabinet mesh or create its parts in the editor. Inspect and edit. Check the size, orientation, drawer interior, and handle opening. Repair missing geometry and keep parts that should move separately. Choose the output. Render an image to show how it looks, or export the part meshes to use in an articulated model. Exported meshes describe the shapes. The URDF model describes their connections and allowed motion. A simulation model also needs contact shapes and physical properties. These applications are alternatives for preparing geometry; a cabinet does not need to pass through all three.

title: 3.1 What is an articulated object?
text: 3.1 What is an articulated object? An articulated object is made of parts that can move relative to one another. A drawer slides. A door swings. The cabinet holds them together. The cabinet below has two independent movements: the drawer slides and the door rotates. Its connections determine which movements are possible. Watch the cabinet animation. Body Stays fixed in this example. Drawer Slides in and out along a straight line. Door Rotates around its hinge.

title: Links and joints
text: 3.1.1 Links and joints We describe this cabinet using two building blocks: links and joints . Link A rigid part: its shape stays the same as it moves. The body, drawer, and door are three links. Joint A connection that defines how two links can move relative to each other. The door’s hinge connects the door to the body and lets it rotate. Both handles are fixed: the drawer handle belongs to the drawer link, and the door handle belongs to the door link. Each moves together with its part.

title: How joints let parts move
text: 3.1.2 How joints let parts move The drawer and door move in different ways. Move the sliders to try each joint. Sliding Prismatic joint Drawer opening 20 cm 0 cm 76 cm The direction stays the same. Only the distance changes. Rotating Revolute joint Door opening 35° 0° 90° The hinge stays in place. Only the angle changes. The allowed range is the joint’s motion limit . The teaching cabinet allows the drawer to open from 0 to 76 cm and the door from 0° to 90°.

title: Degrees of freedom
text: 3.1.3 Degrees of freedom One articulated object can have several degrees of freedom. This cabinet is one object, but it has two movable joints: one for the drawer and one for the door. A degree of freedom (DOF) is an independent motion you can control. With the cabinet body held fixed: Part Independent control DOF Drawer How far it slides 1 Door How far it rotates 1 Whole cabinet Drawer and door move independently 2 You can leave the door still and move the drawer. You can also leave the drawer still and move the door. So describing the whole cabinet’s pose takes two numbers : the drawer’s opening distance and the door’s opening angle. Here, each joint has 1 DOF; the whole cabinet has 2 DOF. Opening the drawer farther changes its position, but it still has the same one degree of freedom.

title: Kinematic trees
text: 3.1.4 Kinematic trees A kinematic tree records which parts are connected. Each node is a link; each connecting line is a joint. The body is the root : the starting link of this tree. It is the parent of the drawer and door; they are its children . The tree describes connections, not the parts’ positions on the page. The same cabinet has two movable joints : a slide for the drawer and a hinge for the door. Each handle is fixed to its part and moves with it. Select a part in the tree, then play its motion. The object The cabinet has a sliding drawer and a hinged door. Its connections hinge slide Body Door Drawer Drawer. Slides relative to the body. Its handle stays attached and moves with it. Play drawer motion Motion position Reset Parts on separate branches move independently The drawer and door are on separate branches of the body. Moving the drawer leaves the door in place; opening the door leaves the drawer in place. Both handles belong to their respective links, so they add no separate movement. The cabinet still has 2 DOF . Not every articulated object forms a tree. Some mechanisms contain closed loops. This example focuses on a tree, where each link other than the root has one parent.

title: 3.2 From 3D shape to a movable object
text: 3.2 From 3D shape to a movable object A reconstructed cabinet can look convincing from several views. To open its drawer, we also need to describe which part moves, how it is connected, and how it responds to a pull.

title: What reconstruction gives us
text: 3.2.1 What reconstruction gives us A 3D reconstruction describes an object’s shape or appearance from photographs. A generated asset proposes a model from an input such as an image. Either result can show a cabinet without identifying its moving parts. These outputs describe shape or appearance. They do not automatically tell us that the blue drawer should slide independently of the cabinet body, or how far a pull will move it. In this example, we use meshes for the visible parts. A 3D editor such as Blender or Maya can help separate or rebuild those parts and check their size. A closed-cabinet reconstruction may omit the drawer’s hidden tray or the space inside the body; those details need to be checked and, where necessary, added. Section 3.6 introduces research methods that help build this structure: Articulate AnyMesh [ 1 ] starts with an existing mesh, while URDFormer [ 2 ] assembles parts from an image and detected part locations.

title: From a cabinet shape to moving parts
text: 3.2.2 What makes the drawer movable? The drawer is a separate moving part. Its front, tray, and handle move together. A sliding joint connects the drawer to the body and restricts it to moving along the rails. Its limit specifies how far it is allowed to open. This is an articulated object : parts connected by joints that describe their relative movement. The joint still does not say what happens under a particular pull. That also depends on properties such as mass and friction, and on contact with other objects. Those are inputs to a physics simulation.

title: Shape, articulation, and simulation
text: 3.2.3 From shape to motion Shape Describe the cabinet’s surfaces, including the drawer tray and handle. Articulation Separate its parts and describe their joints, directions, and limits. Simulation Prepare contact and physical properties, apply a force, and calculate the movement. For the drawer, the distinction is concrete: shape describes the drawer and handle; articulation lets the drawer slide; simulation calculates how it moves when pulled.

title: 3.3 Frames, orientation & URDF
text: 3.3 Frames, orientation & URDF A model needs more than its shape. We also need to know which way it faces, where its joints are, and what each position is measured from.

title: The base and the world
text: 3.3.1 The base and the world A coordinate frame is a reference point with three directions: X, Y, and Z. Its reference point is the origin . World frame The scene’s reference. It lets us place the whole cabinet in a room. Base frame The object’s reference, attached to its root link. Here we use the cabinet body as the base. Move the whole cabinet: its base frame moves with it. The room’s world frame stays in place. The base is not necessarily the object’s bottom or its geometric center. Choosing a base also does not lock the object in place. Holding it fixed is a separate choice in the simulator.

title: Which way is up? Which way is front?
text: 3.3.2 Which way is up? Which way is front? For this chapter’s diagrams, we choose +Z up, +X front, and +Y left in the object’s base frame. “Left” is the object’s own left when facing forward. Other models may use different axes for up and front. First find the object’s usual upright pose. Then use its function to choose the front. Left–right symmetry can suggest an orientation, but it does not always distinguish front from back. Cabinet The side you open is the front. An outward drawer motion is a useful clue. Eyeglasses Use how they are worn: here, front points away from the wearer, through the lenses. The arms extend toward the back. Unmarked box Shape alone may not reveal a unique front. Choose a convention and record it.

title: From a tree to a URDF file
text: 3.3.3 From a tree to a URDF file URDF stands for Unified Robot Description Format. It is a text file that records links and joints, along with their geometry and other properties. Despite its name, it can describe a cabinet too. A joint names its parent and child links. Its type gives the motion rule, axis gives the motion direction in the joint frame, and limit gives the allowed range. Its origin places the joint frame relative to the parent. Before placing the drawer, let’s look at how its shape is stored.

title: What is a mesh?
text: 3.3.4 What is a mesh? A mesh describes a 3D shape using points and flat faces. For the drawer’s orange side panel, those points are its corners. The faces join the points to form its surface. The whole drawer Its sides, bottom, front, and handle move together as one link. One side panel This is one of the drawer’s shapes. The panel’s mesh The file records the points’ positions and which points form each face. The second and third pictures show the same panel . The dots and lines reveal how its shape is represented; they are not extra physical pieces. Several meshes can belong to one link. Here, the drawer’s shape files describe what to draw, while its joint tells the whole drawer how to slide.

title: Joint, link, and visual origins
text: 3.3.5 Joint, link, and visual origins Now place the drawer in the cabinet. The body is the parent link and the drawer is the child link . URDF needs to know where the drawer starts and where to draw its shapes. Body Drawer One side panel O The body’s starting point We measure positions on the cabinet from here. In this model, the points in the drawer’s shape files were also measured from O. J The drawer’s starting point The drawer uses J as its own zero point. At this closed position, J is also the joint’s starting point. The shape files still use O as their zero. The visual origin tells URDF where that saved zero is relative to J. O → J Joint origin Start at the body’s origin O. Where is the drawer’s starting point J? The joint origin gives that offset. J → O Visual origin, in this model Now start at J. Where is the mesh file’s old zero point O? The visual origin gives the offset back, so the panel is placed correctly around the drawer. The cabinet uses O as its zero point; the drawer uses J as its zero point. In this closed pose, the two frames point the same way. The offsets O → J and J → O are therefore equal and opposite: their coordinates add to zero.

title: 3.4 Reading a URDF file
text: 3.4 Reading a URDF file A URDF file [ 1 ] tells us what the parts are, what they look like, and how they connect. We use a URDF of the same teaching cabinet shown throughout the book.

title: One file, parts and connections
text: 3.4.1 One file, parts and connections The whole model sits inside <robot> . Inside it, <link> describes a part, and <joint> connects two parts. The word “robot” is simply the format’s name for the whole model; this one is a cabinet. A pair such as <link> … </link> marks the beginning and end of a block. A tag ending in /> is complete on its own. The file’s outline <robot name="cabinet"> <link name="base" /> <link name="link_2"> … </link> <link name="link_0"> … </link> <link name="link_1"> … </link> <joint name="joint_2" type="fixed"> … </joint> <joint name="joint_0" type="prismatic"> … </joint> <joint name="joint_1" type="revolute"> … </joint> </robot> This outline leaves out the details. Each … stands for lines inside that block. The connections it describes base Reference link · no shape joint_2 · fixed ↓ Cabinet body link_2 joint_0 · slides ↓ Drawer link_0 joint_1 · rotates ↓ Door link_1 The file lists the parts; the joints make the tree. The drawer’s link is not written inside the body’s link. A joint connects them by naming one as its parent and the other as its child . Names such as link_0 are identifiers. Here they mean “drawer”; another model could use drawer directly. What matters is using the same name when referring to that part.

title: Link: shapes that move together
text: 3.4.2 Link: shapes that move together The drawer’s sides, bottom, front, and handle all move together, so they belong to one link . A link can contain several <visual> blocks, each describing a shape to draw. ⤢ These five pieces form the drawer front. They move together as part of one drawer , so they share one sliding joint. Reading one visual block This excerpt describes the red top strip in the picture. The excerpt uses the shared teaching cabinet’s coordinates. <link name="link_0"> <visual name="drawer-front-top-rail"> <origin xyz="0 -0.53 -0.46" /> <geometry> <mesh filename="textured_objs/original-34.obj" /> </geometry> </visual> <!-- The other drawer shapes go here too. --> </link> link The whole drawer. All shapes inside this link follow the drawer’s motion. visual One visible shape belonging to that drawer. origin Places this shape relative to the drawer’s own zero point. geometry mesh Describes the shape. Here, mesh tells the viewer which 3D shape file to open. <geometry> can also contain a simple <box> , <cylinder> , or <sphere> . A separate mesh file is not required for every shape. This drawer has 12 visual blocks but only one sliding joint . More shape files do not mean more degrees of freedom.

title: Joint: let the drawer slide
text: 3.4.3 Joint: let the drawer slide A <joint> answers a different question: how can this part move relative to the part it is attached to? Here the body is the parent, and the drawer is the child. <joint name="joint_0" type="prismatic"> <parent link="link_2" /> <child link="link_0" /> <origin xyz="0 0.53 0.46" /> <axis xyz="0 0 1" /> <limit lower="0" upper="0.76" /> </joint> type Prismatic means sliding. The drawer moves along a straight line. parent child Connect the body ( link_2 ) to the drawer ( link_0 ). origin Locates the joint’s starting frame relative to the body. The red dot marks the drawer’s starting point when closed, called J in the previous chapter. axis 0 0 1 means the joint’s positive Z direction. For this drawer, that points outward. limit The allowed travel is 0 to 0.76 meters : from closed to 76 cm open. ⤢ The dashed outline marks the closed drawer. Here, q = 76 cm : the blue drawer is fully open. One degree of freedom, one number The drawer’s sliding joint has one degree of freedom : it lets the drawer move in and out. One number is enough to describe its position. We call that number q , the distance the drawer has opened. q = 0 cm: the drawer is closed. q = 30 cm: it is partly open. q = 76 cm: it is fully open in this model. The limit sets the allowed range, 0–76 cm . The value of q tells us where the drawer is right now within that range.

title: Joint: let the door rotate
text: 3.4.4 Joint: let the door rotate The door uses the same structure, with a different motion type. Revolute means a hinge with a limited angle. <joint name="joint_1" type="revolute"> <parent link="link_2" /> <child link="link_1" /> <origin xyz="-0.51 -0.73 0.46" /> <axis xyz="0 -1 0" /> <limit lower="0" upper="1.5708" /> </joint> The origin places the joint’s starting point at the hinge. The axis gives the direction of the hinge line through that point. Here 0 -1 0 points downward in the joint’s frame. ⤢ The door turns around the purple hinge line . The dashed outline shows it closed. Here, q = 90° : the solid door is fully open. Rotating joints use radians in the file: 1.5708 radians is approximately 90° . So this door is allowed to open from 0° to 90°. The picture shows it at that upper limit. This hinge also has one degree of freedom . For the door, q is the opening angle ; for the drawer, q is the opening distance. A wheel that can keep turning without an angular stop would use type="continuous" instead. It has a rotation axis but no lower or upper position limit.

title: How a part looks and behaves
text: 3.4.5 How a part looks and behaves A link can describe three things about a part, such as this cabinet body: visual The shape you see. Draws the cabinet body and the shelf inside it. collision The shape used to check contact. For example, it tells the simulator whether a box touches the shelf. inertial How heavy the part is and how its mass is spread out. Helps calculate how it responds to pushes and turns. ⤢ This shelf uses the same 3D shape for visual and collision : one shape for drawing it and checking contact. This cabinet file includes visual and collision data. It has no inertial blocks, so it does not specify how heavy the parts are.

title: Why is there an extra base link?
text: 3.4.6 Why is there an extra base link? Our cabinet has three visible parts, yet the file has four links. The extra one is base , an invisible reference for the whole cabinet . The fixed joint joint_2 places the cabinet body relative to that reference. <link name="base" /> <joint name="joint_2" type="fixed"> <parent link="base" /> <child link="link_2" /> <origin xyz="0 0 0" rpy="1.5708 0 -1.5708" /> </joint> A fixed joint can set an orientation The rpy numbers store a rotation. In this example, that rotation turns the cabinet body into the intended orientation. Fixed means the body keeps that orientation relative to the base. There is no extra movement to control. ⤢ Both the middle and right examples remove the base and fixed joint. The right example takes one extra step: it rotates the whole cabinet in the scene to restore the original orientation. These pictures show starting poses, before any physics simulation. Can we leave out the base and fixed joint? Yes, with two steps: remove both elements so the cabinet body becomes the root, then apply the original fixed joint’s rotation to the whole cabinet when placing it in the scene. The drawer and door can then move exactly as before. Keeping base and joint_2 stores the rotation inside the URDF. Removing both moves that responsibility to how we place the model in the scene. What if we remove only the fixed joint? The base link would be left disconnected from the cabinet. We would have two separate roots: base and the cabinet body. A URDF needs one connected tree, so a standard URDF loader rejects this arrangement. None of the three pictures shows this disconnected case. The fixed joint adds zero degrees of freedom . With the cabinet held still, the drawer and door still provide two independent movements: one slide and one rotation. Teaching cabinet URDF URDF + mesh files URDF reference ↗

title: 3.5 What happens when we change the URDF?
text: 3.5 What happens when we change the URDF? Use the same cabinet to see what changes when we edit its joints and shapes. [ 1 ]

title: Change the drawer’s direction
text: 3.5.1 Change the drawer’s direction The drawer’s axis tells it which way to slide. Here we change only that direction. The starting point and the 0–76 cm travel range stay the same. The +X, +Y, and +Z arrows show the joint’s reference directions at its closed pose. In this cabinet, +X points sideways, +Y points up, and +Z points out of the front . These are the joint’s local axes; the scene can use a different up axis. The purple arrow shows the chosen sliding direction. Out of the cabinet ⤢ <axis xyz=" 0 0 1 " /> 0 0 1 means +Z: increasing q pulls the drawer outward. Into the cabinet ⤢ <axis xyz=" 0 0 -1 " /> 0 0 −1 means −Z: the purple arrow points opposite +Z. Keeping the same positive range now sends the drawer inward. Along a diagonal ⤢ The purple arrow combines +X and +Y : sideways and upward together. <axis xyz=" 0.707107 0.707107 0 " /> Read xyz in order: X, then Y, then Z . The two equal positive numbers mean “move sideways along +X and upward along +Y by equal amounts.” The final 0 means no movement along Z. For example, after sliding 10 cm along the purple arrow, the drawer has moved about 7.1 cm sideways and 7.1 cm upward . This is still one degree of freedom. The drawer follows one straight line. It cannot choose its upward and sideways movements separately. One number, q , tells us how far it has moved along that line. The cabinet is transparent so you can see the path. These animations follow the motion written in the file; they do not stop parts at collisions.

title: Turn a hinged door into a sliding door
text: 3.5.2 Turn a hinged door into a sliding door For a hinge, axis gives the line the door rotates around . For a slide, it gives the direction the door moves along . Changing revolute to prismatic also changes the limit from an angle to a distance. Original hinged door ⤢ type="revolute" <axis xyz="0 -1 0" /> <limit lower="0" upper="1.5708" /> 0 −1 0 points along −Y , down the vertical hinge. The door turns around that line. 1.5708 radians is about 90°. Change only the type ⤢ type=" prismatic " <axis xyz="0 -1 0" /> <limit lower="0" upper="1.5708" /> The same −Y axis now means slide downward . The same upper limit now means 1.5708 meters . This movement is set by the joint, not by gravity. Make it slide sideways ⤢ 1 0 0 means +X: the door slides sideways across the front of the cabinet. type=" prismatic " <axis xyz=" 1 0 0 " /> <limit lower="0" upper=" 0.7 " /> We change three things together: Type: slide instead of rotate. Axis: move sideways instead of downward. Limit: travel 70 cm. The door still has one DOF . Its q now measures distance instead of angle.

title: Remove the drawer
text: 3.5.3 Remove the drawer To remove this drawer, delete both its link and the joint connecting it to the cabinet . With the drawer ⤢ Cabinet body ├── Drawer · joint_0 └── Door · joint_1 Two movable parts: the drawer and the door. Without the drawer ⤢ Cabinet body └── Door · joint_1 The door still works. The drawer opening remains because it is part of the cabinet body. In this file, remove the entire <link name="link_0"> block and the entire <joint name="joint_0"> block. Deleting only the link would leave a joint pointing to a drawer that no longer exists. Deleting only the joint would leave the drawer disconnected. This drawer has no parts attached beneath it in the tree, so the other connections can stay as they are.

title: Swap the shapes, keep the joints
text: 3.5.4 Swap the shapes, keep the joints What if the drawer used the door’s joint, and the door used the drawer’s joint? Original shapes ⤢ The blue drawer slides. The gold door swings. Shapes swapped ⤢ The blue drawer shape swings. The gold door panel slides. The joint sets the movement, whatever shape we attach to it. Calling a link “drawer” or giving it a drawer shape does not automatically make it slide. Link and joint Original shape New shape link_0 · sliding joint Drawer Door panel link_1 · hinge joint Door panel Drawer For this example, we exchange the two links’ visual and collision blocks. We also adjust their placement offsets so both shapes still start in the same closed positions. The joints keep their original locations, directions, and limits. The result is an unusual cabinet, but it makes the roles clear: the shapes describe the parts; the joints describe their movement. Teaching cabinet URDF URDF + mesh files URDF reference ↗

title: 3.6 Automatically build articulated models
text: 3.6 Automatically build articulated models An articulated cabinet needs separate parts and joints: the drawer slides relative to the body, and the door rotates around a hinge. Research methods can help infer this structure. Articulate AnyMesh starts with a 3D mesh; URDFormer starts with an image and detected part locations. The links and joints introduced in Section 3.1 are the information these methods aim to recover. We follow the same cabinet through each method’s input, processing steps, output, and checks.

title: Articulate AnyMesh: from a mesh to moving parts
text: 3.6.1 Articulate AnyMesh: from a mesh to moving parts Articulate AnyMesh [ 1 ] adds part identities and joints to an existing 3D object. It combines a vision-language model (VLM) , part-segmentation tools, and geometry calculations. The project page shows the authors’ results. Input A cabinet mesh . Its surfaces already describe the cabinet’s shape. This mesh could come from an editor, a generator such as TRELLIS or Hunyuan3D , or surface reconstruction such as the 2DGS mesh extraction in Section 2.8 . Workflow Articulate AnyMesh: from a mesh to moving parts 01 Cabinet mesh Existing surfaces before adding movement. 02 Identify parts and joints VLM judgments and geometry calculations locate parts and their movement. 03 Articulated asset The drawer slides; the door rotates. Shape and appearance are also refined. Colors in the middle identify groups of 3D surfaces . The drawer front, tray, and handle form one moving part. These scripted cabinet views explain the stages; the research method’s predictions can differ. Processing steps Identify and separate parts. GPT-4o [ 2 ] interprets rendered views of the mesh. A part-segmentation pipeline, PartSlip++ [ 3 ] , combines detections and masks from several views into 3D part groups. Propose the movement structure. GPT-4o uses the recognized object and parts to propose parent–child connections and joint types, such as a sliding drawer and a hinged door. Locate the motion axes. Geometry calculations and further model judgments determine where those movements take place, as illustrated below. Refine the asset. A diffusion-based method, RichDreamer [ 4 ] , helps refine shape and appearance across different joint positions. The paper’s method section describes these components. How the drawer and door get their joints First choose a type of movement; then locate its axis. A sliding joint needs a direction. A rotating joint needs both the direction and position of its hinge line. The drawer. GPT-4o proposes a sliding joint and classifies its movement as inward/outward. The program fits a plane to the region where the drawer and body are close together, then uses the direction perpendicular to that plane as the sliding axis. On this cabinet, that gives the direction through the front opening. The door. GPT-4o proposes a rotating joint. The program marks candidate 3D points on a rendered view; the model selects points likely to lie on the hinge. A line fitted through the selected points becomes the estimated rotation axis. On this cabinet, the intended axis runs vertically along the door’s left edge. The published prompts show the judgments requested from GPT-4o. Joint estimation Choose a joint, then locate its axis Articulate AnyMesh Drawer Door 01 Model prediction Model prediction Slide inward / outward GPT-4o proposes a sliding joint. Model prediction Rotate around a hinge GPT-4o proposes rotation and selects hinge candidates A and B. 02 Locate the axis Drawer Slide direction Perpendicular to the illustrated connection plane. Door Vertical hinge Selected candidates A and B lie along the left hinge. 03 Program step Geometry calculation Calculate a direction Fit the connection plane; use its perpendicular direction as the slide axis. Geometry calculation Fit a hinge line Fit a line through the selected 3D points to obtain the rotation axis. The labels distinguish model predictions from geometry calculations. The plane and candidate points are authored guides on the shared cabinet. Output An articulated 3D asset : part geometry with estimated connections and joint information. The project’s robot demonstration exports this structure as a URDF with part meshes . As in Section 3.4 , the URDF describes the links and joints, while the mesh files describe their shapes. What to check Move the drawer and door through their intended ranges. Check the part boundaries, sliding direction, hinge location, and the hidden surfaces exposed by opening them. Each fixed handle should move with its drawer or door. Section 3.5 illustrates how changes to the joint or mesh affect movement.

title: URDFormer: from an image to an assembled model
text: 3.6.2 URDFormer: from an image to an assembled model URDFormer [ 5 ] combines a part detector, a trained structure-prediction network, and assembly rules. Its network learns from paired images and scene descriptions. At use time, the predictions select and arrange prepared meshes in a URDF model. The project page shows single objects and larger scenes. Input A cabinet image and bounding boxes around its visible parts . A bounding box is a rectangle marking a part’s location in the picture. The pipeline’s detector supplies these boxes—for example, around a drawer or handle—and URDFormer uses them together with the image. Workflow URDFormer: from an image to an assembled model 01 Image + part boxes Detected rectangles locate visible parts in the picture. 02 Predict, then assemble Predicted drawer category Select a drawer mesh Position, size, parent Place it in the upper cabinet body Program rules assign the category’s joints and write the URDF. 03 URDF + part meshes A proposed 3D arrangement with movable parts. The rectangles mark 2D image regions . The middle lists examples of predicted attributes. title: Two routes to an articulated cabinet
text: 3.6.3 Two routes to an articulated cabinet Where the two methods begin and how they build the result Stage Articulate AnyMesh URDFormer Input An existing 3D mesh. For a cabinet photograph, URDFormer provides a route to assembling an articulated model from prepared parts. Both aim to produce a structure whose parts can move relative to one another. title: 4.1 From animation to simulation
text: 4.1 From animation to simulation A box moves down toward a table. We can create that movement in two different ways. This chapter develops physical motion, scene preparation, and robot control. The software map in Section 4.5 shows how physics engines such as MuJoCo [ 1 ] connect to task environments such as ManiSkill and RoboCasa. Simulation also involves choosing useful shape detail. A cabinet can have a detailed mesh for its appearance and simpler collision shapes for calculating where objects touch. Section 4.2 explains this choice : simplify where possible while preserving the drawer cavity and the opening behind the handle.

title: Two ways to move a box
text: 4.1.1 Two ways to move a box We choose the positions “Start here. Move down. Stop here.” The box follows the positions we chose. We do not calculate gravity or contact for this animation. We calculate the motion “Put the box here, then let go.” The simulator calculates the movement. Gravity makes the box fall; contact with the table stops it. Table height 40 cm Lower Higher Gravity on Both boxes reach the table. Raise the table to see the difference. Both examples repeat from the same starting position. The box on the right starts at rest, with no air resistance or bounce. The interactive comparison needs JavaScript. The explanations below describe what each change would do.

title: Change the scene
text: 4.1.2 Change the scene Raise the table On the left, the box keeps following its saved path. It passes through the raised tabletop because we have not changed its positions or added a contact rule. On the right, the box meets the higher table sooner and rests on its surface. The simulator calculates a new result from the changed scene. Turn gravity off On the left, the saved movement continues. On the right, the box stays where we release it. It starts with no speed, and there is now no force pulling it down. We could edit the left animation to match either result. With the simulation, we change the scene or its physical settings and calculate the movement again.

title: Back to the drawer
text: 4.1.3 Back to the drawer The cabinet GIFs in Chapter 3 work like the box on the left. We choose the drawer’s opening distance, q , at each moment: closed, a little open, farther open, and back again. To simulate a pull, we give the drawer mass, describe friction, and apply a pulling force. Its joint still restricts it to sliding. The simulator calculates how fast it moves and how its opening distance changes. The examples below do this. Chapter 3 animations We choose q → draw the drawer there. Physics simulation We apply a pull → calculate the movement → get q. A simulation can also produce an animation. Either result can be saved as a GIF or video. The difference is how the positions were produced. A falling-box example in MuJoCo ↗

title: Pull the drawer
text: 4.1.4 Pull the drawer A force is a push or a pull. We measure it in newtons, written N . A 3 N pull is three times as strong as a 1 N pull. It does not tell us how many centimeters the drawer will open. Here we pull each drawer for half a second , then let go. Both start closed and still. Both have a mass of 2 kg, and we leave out friction for this first comparison. ⤢ The stronger pull makes the same drawer gain speed faster. After the same amount of time, it has opened farther. The green arrow shows the pull; the blue measurement shows q. We chose the force, not the ending position. The opening distances come from calculating the motion and drawing each resulting position. These are side-view teaching examples with chosen values, not measurements of the earlier cabinet. The cabinet stays fixed, and its rails keep the drawer moving horizontally. Only forces along the slide are shown. The GIFs play slowly and hold their last frame before replaying.

title: Same pull, different mass
text: 4.1.5 Same pull, different mass Now keep the pull the same: 3 N for half a second . Change only the moving mass, from 2 kg to 4 kg . Think of adding items to the drawer. Friction is still left out so we can see the effect of mass by itself. ⤢ The heavier drawer gains speed more slowly under the same pull. It opens less during this example. This is why the simulator needs mass. Two drawers can look identical and have the same sliding joint, yet respond differently to the same pull.

title: Friction can resist the pull
text: 4.1.6 Friction can resist the pull Have you pulled a drawer gently and found that it would not budge? Friction can balance a weak pull and keep the drawer still. Once the drawer slides, friction acts against that sliding movement. Both drawers below have a mass of 2 kg and receive the same 3 N pull . Only the friction in their rails changes. ⤢ Green points in the pulling direction. Orange shows friction pushing against the pull or the sliding movement. The easy-sliding drawer starts moving, with 0.8 N of friction opposing the 3 N pull. The stiff rails can resist a pull of up to 4 N before sliding starts . With our 3 N pull, their friction only needs to provide 3 N in the opposite direction. The forces balance, so that drawer stays still. Applying a force does not guarantee movement. We have to account for the other forces too.

title: What happens after letting go?
text: 4.1.7 What happens after letting go? Removing the pull does not instantly stop a moving drawer. In this example, both drawers are already moving outward at 40 cm per second . They are both 10 cm open when we let go. ⤢ Without friction or another opposing force, the drawer keeps its speed. With friction, it slows down and stops. Neither drawer reaches its 76 cm travel limit in this clip. The drawer does not automatically close when we let go. That would need something else, such as a spring or a closing force. Here, each replay simply restarts the example. The sliding joint still has one degree of freedom : q tells us the opening distance. The force changes how q develops over time; it does not add another degree of freedom. Force and mass ↗ Friction ↗ Motion after release ↗ [ 2 ]

title: 4.2 Preparing a simulation model
text: 4.2 Preparing a simulation model Chapter 3 described the cabinet’s parts and allowed movements. A force experiment also needs shapes for contact, physical properties, and a starting pose. This section prepares those inputs for the simulator.

title: Choose useful shape detail
text: Choose useful shape detail Mesh resolution refers to how finely the surface is divided into vertices and faces. Image resolution describes the number of pixels in a picture. More closely spaced faces can follow a curved handle, while a flat cabinet wall can be represented with a few large faces. A detailed visible mesh can make the cabinet look convincing. For contact calculations, we can supply a simpler collision shape : the geometry the simulator uses to decide where objects touch. More complex collision geometry can increase calculation time, so it is useful to keep only the detail needed for the task. The visible mesh can remain detailed. For a drawer-opening test, the collision shapes represent the cabinet walls, drawer, and handle, with open space for the drawer to slide and a finger to reach behind the grip. Small decorative grooves can be kept in the visible mesh. Collision geometry preserves the details that affect contact and movement; visual geometry preserves the details needed for the picture. Using separate shapes lets us choose an appropriate level of detail for each purpose. MuJoCo’s modeling guide [ 1 ] describes how to configure them.

title: Separate the cabinet into bodies and joints
text: 4.2.1 Separate the moving parts If the whole cabinet is treated as one rigid body, pulling the handle cannot open the drawer independently. We need a separate drawer body connected to the cabinet body . The drawer front, tray, and handle move together. They belong to one moving body even if they use several shapes. A joint describes the allowed movement between bodies. Give the drawer a sliding joint along its rails and a maximum opening distance. A door would use a hinge joint instead. For our first test, hold the cabinet body and door still and study only the drawer. We also check size and orientation here. A model that is accidentally one hundred times too large will not describe the same physical cabinet. These parts, their connections, and their allowed movements are the subject of Chapter 3 .

title: Create collision shapes from the part meshes, then check the empty space
text: 4.2.2 Define where contact happens Section 3.2.1 introduced the cabinet mesh, and Section 4.2.1 identified its moving parts. At this point in the example, we have the part meshes but have not yet prepared separate collision shapes. Preparing them is the new task in this section. The part meshes supply the visible shapes used to draw the cabinet. A collision shape is geometry supplied to the simulator to calculate where objects touch. From one cabinet wall to a collision box Start with the wall’s mesh. Use its dimensions and position as a guide. Define a box that matches that wall. Give it the wall’s height, width, thickness, and position. This box is the collision shape for the wall in this example. Save that definition in the simulation model file. A person or a program can write the box’s dimensions and placement. The simulator reads that definition to create the box it uses for contact calculations. This box does not need a separate mesh file. Its dimensions and placement are enough to describe it. More complex collision shapes can use mesh files instead. In either case, the shape is an input prepared before contact testing ; the test calculates contacts using that shape. MuJoCo’s shape definitions. Leave room for the drawer Repeat this for the cabinet’s walls. Each box represents wall material, leaving the interior empty. One box around the entire cabinet would incorrectly fill the drawer’s space: One box around the cabinet: the drawer’s space is treated as solid. Boxes along the walls: the drawer has room between them. The top is removed in these drawings so we can see inside. Check, adjust, and check again A visual check: display the collision shapes in the viewer and inspect the interior. Look at the boxes themselves, because the detailed visible mesh can hide an incorrectly filled space. A programmed check: a script can place the drawer at several opening distances and check for unwanted overlaps with the cabinet. The relevant collision checks must be enabled. If a check finds a problem, revise the collision shapes: For boxes: change their dimensions or positions in the model file, by hand or with a program. If one large box fills the cabinet interior, replace it with separate wall boxes. For collision meshes: edit the geometry in Blender, or use a program to modify or regenerate it, then save the updated mesh. Reload the updated model and repeat the checks. The goal is to represent the actual walls and handle while keeping their intended openings clear. The tests use the shapes we prepared; they do not produce those shapes from contact results. The same idea applies to the handle : its collision shapes must leave the gap behind the bar open for a finger. Shapes representing the drawer and its handle belong to the drawer, so they move with it. Once these shape checks pass, continue to the motion test: Section 4.2.3 adds mass and friction, and Section 4.3.2 applies a pull. Passing the shape checks prepares the model for that test; the pull test then checks its movement.

title: Add mass, resistance, and a starting state
text: 4.2.3 Add physical properties Joints define the drawer’s allowed movement, and collision shapes define where contact can occur. Physical properties determine its response to a pull: an empty drawer and a loaded drawer can have the same visible shape but move differently. The force tests described here run in MuJoCo on a computer. A Python test script—a small program—loads the cabinet model, applies a chosen force, and records the resulting motion. MuJoCo’s viewer can show the moving cabinet. Section 4.3.1 describes this setup. Mass How much mass moves with the drawer? The same pull accelerates a heavier drawer less. Mass distribution Where is that mass located? This affects resistance to changes in rotation, called rotational inertia . It matters for a rotating door and other moving bodies. Resistance How strongly do the rails resist sliding? We can model rail friction and damping. If a gripper holds the handle, contact friction also affects whether it slips. Starting state Is the drawer closed? Is it already moving? Our test starts closed and at rest, with the cabinet body held fixed. For a simple test, we might choose a 2 kg drawer with a 50 cm travel limit . These are teaching values. To represent a real cabinet, measure or estimate its properties and check them against observed movement. A nice reconstruction alone does not tell us its mass or rail friction. Store the bodies, joints, geometry, and physical settings in the simulator’s model description. MuJoCo uses MJCF , an XML model format. URDF , introduced in Chapter 3 , is another format for describing links and joints; importing a URDF can still require simulator-specific preparation. MuJoCo’s model formats.

title: 4.3 MuJoCo experiments
text: 4.3 MuJoCo experiments The model from Section 4.2 describes the cabinet. A test script loads it, applies a chosen force, and asks MuJoCo [ 1 ] to calculate the motion. Those calculated positions can then be rendered as a video.

title: Set up the experiment
text: 4.3.1 Set up the experiment One practical setup uses MuJoCo with a Python test script on a computer: The model file describes the cabinet: its parts, joints, collision shapes, mass, and resistance. The Python script sets up the test: load the model, start the drawer closed and still, apply the chosen pulling force for a set duration, and ask MuJoCo to advance the simulation. MuJoCo calculates the motion: the script can record opening distance and speed, while a viewer window displays the cabinet moving. For a mass comparison, load the 2 kg version and run the pull. Then load the 4 kg version and repeat from the same starting state, keeping the force, geometry, and resistance settings unchanged. The two runs show how the assumed mass affects the result. MuJoCo’s Python interface and viewer.

title: Calculate the drawer’s motion
text: 4.3.2 Calculate the drawer’s motion For a simple experiment, start with the drawer closed and still. Apply an outward 3 N force for 0.5 seconds , then remove that force. A newton (N) measures force. Continue the simulation until 2 seconds of simulated time to observe what happens after the pull ends. These are example settings for the experiment. MuJoCo calculates the motion in small time steps. At each step, the drawer has an opening distance and a speed; together, these describe its state . “Current” and “next” refer to the same drawer at two nearby times, not simply to “closed” and “open.” Workflow Advance one small time step 01 Now Drawer opening and speed now 02 Calculate a small step Use the current force, mass, resistance, contacts, and joint limits 03 A moment later Opening and speed a small time step later Continue from that new opening and speed. Each step advances time a little; this experiment stops at 2 seconds. Ending the pull does not end the simulation. After 0.5 seconds, the applied pulling force is zero, but the drawer may still be moving. Later steps calculate whether it slows down, stops, or reaches its joint limit. The experiment chooses when to stop stepping. Here it stops at 2 seconds, even if the drawer is still moving. Another test could stop when a target opening is reached, with a time limit if it never gets there. MuJoCo’s simulation loop.

title: Record opening distance over time
text: 4.3.3 Record opening distance over time At each step, we can record the time, the drawer’s opening distance q , and its speed. Together, these records describe its motion over time : how far it opened during the pull and what happened after release. Section 4.1 shows calculated drawer examples. The allowed range , such as 0–50 cm, is an input specified by the joint. The actual opening at each moment is a result of the simulation. A 50 cm limit does not mean this pull will open the drawer by 50 cm. These calculated positions are the input to Section 4.3.4 : the renderer draws the cabinet at each saved position to make the frames of a video.

title: Turn the calculated positions into images
text: 4.3.4 Turn the calculated positions into images Section 4.3.3 gives opening distances over time. To make a video frame, place the visible drawer at the position calculated for that frame’s time. A renderer uses those shapes, their appearance, lighting, and a camera to make a 2D frame. Save a sequence of frames to make a video. MuJoCo has its own renderer, so a separate rendering application is not required. MuJoCo rendering. Workflow From motion to video frames 01 MuJoCo physics Calculates a new drawer pose 02 Mesh + renderer Draws that pose from a camera 03 2D frame Many frames make a video Changing only the camera makes a different picture of the same state. Changing the pull, mass, or friction can change the movement itself. This is why rendering and physics occupy different places in the workflow. Where all the names fit Workflow From an asset to a simulation video 01 TRELLIS · create the asset Cabinet image → a proposed mesh 02 Blender · prepare the geometry Mesh → separate body, drawer, and door shapes, at the correct scale 03 Model preparation · write an MJCF model Part shapes + joints + collision shapes + physical settings → a simulation model 04 MuJoCo · calculate the movement Simulation model + initial state + pull → positions and speeds over time 05 Renderer · make the pictures Those positions + visible geometry + appearance + camera and lighting → video frames The preparation between a generated mesh and a simulation is real work; a file conversion alone does not complete it. With NeRF or 3DGS, the beginning changes: photos → fit a scene → render new views already gives a visual result. To simulate a moving drawer, add the same physical structure described here. Keeping its learned appearance on moving parts requires an additional way to associate and move that appearance with each part. Finally, check the test: does the drawer follow the rail, stay attached, and stop near its limit? Are there unintended overlaps? If we have a real cabinet, compare the same pull in both. When they disagree, revisit the geometry or physical settings instead of judging the simulation only by how good its video looks.

title: 4.4 Robot interaction and control
text: 4.4 Robot interaction and control The previous experiment applied a force directly to the drawer. To test a robot opening it, the model must also include the arm, gripper, and their contact with the handle.

title: Add the robot to the scene
text: 4.4.1 Add the robot to the scene The direct test supplies a force to the drawer without modeling a hand. To study a grasp, add a robot arm and gripper to the same scene, with their joints, physical properties, and collision shapes. MuJoCo [ 1 ] then simulates both the robot and the cabinet, including contact between them.

title: From an action to a physical response
text: 4.4.2 From an action to a physical response A controller is the program that tries to carry out a requested robot movement. For example, “move the gripper 10 cm outward while keeping it closed” must become control signals for the simulated robot’s motors. The controller uses the robot’s current state to update those signals. Workflow From an action to a physical response 01 Choose an action. A predefined program can request the movement. A VLA can instead propose it from the camera image and an instruction, as in Section 1.3 . 02 The controller tries to execute it. It sends control signals to move the arm and keep the gripper closed. 03 MuJoCo calculates the response. The simulated motors move the robot; contact with the handle can transfer the pull to the drawer. The grip may hold or slip, and the drawer may move or stay stuck. 04 Observe the result. Read the new robot and drawer positions. A renderer can make the next camera image for a VLA to use when choosing another action. A VLA is optional. It is one way to choose actions; a simple programmed sequence can also drive this test. A requested action can span many physics steps, so a new VLA prediction is not required at every step. OpenVLA [ 2 ] is an example action model; MuJoCo’s actuation model describes how control inputs produce simulated forces. The robot test also needs a stopping rule, such as reaching the desired opening or running out of allotted simulated time. Both tests produce motion over time; in the robot test, the pull comes through the modeled robot and its contact with the handle.

title: A research example: reconstruction to robot motion
text: 4.4.3 A research example: reconstruction to robot motion The Articulate AnyMesh project’s real-to-sim-to-real demonstration [ 3 ] connects several steps introduced in this book: Recover a surface. Use 2DGS to reconstruct a real object and extract a mesh, as described in Section 2.8 . Add articulation. Articulate AnyMesh converts the mesh into an articulated URDF; see Section 3.6 . Plan in simulation. Sample action targets and use motion planning to find a trajectory that avoids collisions and completes the task. Execute on the real robot. The authors then replay the trajectory in the physical scene. In the book’s cabinet example, a corresponding task would be to reach the drawer handle and pull it outward. The model supplies the cabinet’s parts and joints; the robot, motion planner, and controller supply the movement used to interact with it. This returns to the task in Chapter 1 : a model can propose an action, a controller tries to carry it out, and the simulated scene determines the resulting motion. The next camera image shows the outcome of that interaction. Section 4.5 places these jobs in software: physics engines, scene frameworks, and the ManiSkill and RoboCasa task environments used for learning and evaluation.
